problems.title: Problem C (Experimental part)
problems.problem:
Problem C (Experimental part)

Bending is in general the result of the action of forces exerted in a suitable way on an elongated body of negligible thickness, such as a metal strip or a flexible plastic ruler.

As the body tends to curve, compression is produced on one of its surfaces and tension (stretching) on the other. Bending causes the deformation or even the fracture of the body.

In the case of the elastic deformation of a thin metal strip, whose deformations are due to external causes, without any contribution to them from the strip's own weight, a distance of its end from its initial direction corresponds, which is called the "deflection" (βέλος κάμψης).

To a satisfactory approximation, we can use for the study of the elastic deformations caused by forces perpendicular to the surface of the strip at one of its ends, while the other end is rigidly fixed, the law of elastic deformations (Hooke's law) in the known form: $|F| = kx$ (1), where k is the "elastic constant" of the strip, which is related to its construction characteristics, and x is the length of the deflection. By extension, for the elastic potential energy that is stored in the deformed strip or released from the deformed strip it will hold: $U = \dfrac{1}{2}kx^2$ (2)

A. A similar strip is fixed with its surface in the vertical plane, with a clamp, at the edge of a table, carefully, so that it does not touch the table but can touch a small cylindrical body (Σ) that is on the surface of the table. For example, the body (Σ) may be made of a few 2€ coins soldered together, and let m be their total mass.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2017-3-3-fig1.png

We cause a small bending of the strip by exerting with our hand a force at the end of the strip, perpendicular to its surface. The strip bends and we can easily measure the value of the deflection x. Because the procedure will be repeated, and so that the measurement is free of random errors each time, instead of exerting the force with our hand we prefer to exert it by means of a string that is tied to the end of the strip and is pulled to a predetermined position. When we burn the string, the strip springs back towards its initial position, where we accept that on colliding with the body (Σ) it transfers to it the whole of the elastic energy that had been stored in it during its bending.

The energy transferred from the strip to the body (Σ) appears in the body in the form of kinetic energy $K = \dfrac{1}{2}m\upsilon_0^2$ (3)

In this way the body (Σ) is launched from the position where it was initially, with initial velocity $\upsilon_0$, and slides without jumping, continuously in contact with the surface of the table, so that, because of the kinetic friction with coefficient μ, it decelerates and finally comes to rest, having covered on the table a distance S, which can easily be measured.

C1. Using the equations for the study of the decelerated motion of the body (Σ), assuming that at the instant $t_0 = 0$ it starts to move with its initial velocity $\upsilon_0$, prove that the following equation holds: $S = \dfrac{kx^2}{2\mu mg}$ (4)

[6 marks]

C2. In a table we can record the values of the quantities x and S that are measured each time the procedure is repeated.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c} x\ (\mathrm{mm}) & 10 & 15 & 20 & 25 & 30 & 35 & 40 \\ \hline S\ (\mathrm{mm}) & 10 & 21 & 34 & 53 & 72 & 98 & 126 \\ \hline x^2\ (\mathrm{mm^2}) & & & & & & & \end{array}$$

After completing the table and using the 2 appropriate rows of the table, so as to represent graphically the distance S covered by the body as a function of the square $x^2$ of the length of the deflection, $S = f(x^2)$, of equation (4), draw a suitable graph on the graph paper. Explain your answer in detail.

[7 marks]

C3. (a) Measure, explaining the method you use, the slope of the graph that you drew.

(b) Find the relation that connects the slope you calculated from the graph with the quantities k, m, g, μ.

[6 marks]

B. We are interested, through a procedure based on the data of the measurements, in calculating the value of the coefficient of kinetic friction μ between the body (Σ) and the surface of the table.

For this purpose we fix the strip so that it projects from the table with its broad surface horizontal. We place the body (Σ) at its end and hold it until, slowly, it reaches equilibrium (at the limit).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2017-3-3-fig2.png

The weight of the body (Σ) has caused bending of the strip, and let y be the value of the deflection along the vertical axis, which can be measured. It was found to be y = 25 mm and approximately it holds: mg = ky (5)

Taking (5) into account, equation (4) becomes: $S = \dfrac{kx^2}{2\mu mg}$ or $S = \dfrac{x^2}{2\mu y}$ (6)

C4. With the help of the slope of the diagram that you calculated and the value of y, explain how you can find the value of the coefficient of kinetic friction μ between the body (Σ) and the surface of the table.

[3 marks]

C5. With a dynamometer we measure the weight of the body (Σ) and find it equal to 0.5 N. Calculate the elastic constant k of the metal strip.

[3 marks]

problems.title: Problem D
problems.problem:
Problem D

A Physics teacher, in order to train his students in the study of the motions of bodies and of Newtonian composition, constructed an inclined plane (i.p.) of length L whose inclination could be varied. In its construction he incorporated a suitable scale, so that at every position of the inclined plane the tangent of the angle that the i.p. makes with the horizontal direction is known. At the end of the inclined plane he fixed a suitable stop, which the bodies will hit after sliding on it, and they will stop almost instantaneously without rebounding backwards. He also constructed two small bodies (1) and (2) of equal mass (which we consider as material points, without dimensions) from different materials, so that they have different coefficients of kinetic friction with the inclined plane. He joined these two bodies by tying them with a massless, inextensible string of length L/2.

D1. First he put to his students the following question: If we know that the magnitude of the tension of the string cannot exceed the magnitude of the weight of each body at the place where the experiments are carried out, and if we place the i.p. in a horizontal position, prove that the ratio of the magnitudes of the forces $F_1$ and $F_2$ for which the string is at the limit of breaking in the cases shown in figure 1 is equal to: $\dfrac{F_1}{F_2} = \dfrac{2+\mu_2-\mu_1}{2+\mu_1-\mu_2}$, where $\mu_1$ and $\mu_2$ are the coefficients of kinetic friction of each body with the i.p.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2017-3-4-fig1.png

Figure 1

[6 marks]

D2. Then, together with the students, he made the following observations:

1. They set the inclination of the i.p. to $\varepsilon\varphi\varphi_1 = 0.4$. They held the bodies at rest at the position shown in figure 2 below, with the string stretched, and released them simultaneously, free to move. They observed that the two bodies started to move immediately, the string remained stretched until body 1 touched the stop, and body 2 reached the stop with zero velocity.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2017-3-4-fig2.png

Figure 2

2. They set the inclination of the i.p. to $\varepsilon\varphi\varphi_2 = 0.9$. They again held the bodies at rest at the position shown in figure 3 below, with the string stretched. They released the bodies simultaneously and observed that the two bodies started to move immediately, the string slackened as soon as they were released, and both bodies reached the stop at the end of the i.p. at the same instant.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2017-3-4-fig3.png

Figure 3

The teacher explained to his students that the two observations above are sufficient for the coefficients of kinetic friction of each body with the i.p. to be calculated. Find the way to calculate them yourselves too, and hence calculate the value of the ratio $\dfrac{F_1}{F_2}$ of question D1.

[7 marks]

D3. Finally, the teacher put to his students the following question. If the coefficient of limiting (maximum static) friction between each body and the floor is 20% greater than the coefficient of kinetic friction, and if we place the bodies on the i.p. as in figure 4, up to what value can the inclination of the i.p. be increased so that neither body starts to slide?

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2017-3-4-fig4.png

Figure 4

[7 marks]

D4. If the same experiments with the same bodies and the same inclined plane were carried out at another place where the gravitational acceleration has a different value, would the observations of the students and the results of your calculations change? Explain.

[5 marks]

problems.title: Problem A. Multiple-choice questions without justification
problems.problem:
Problem A. Multiple-choice questions without justification

1. An observer "hears" the beats from the superposition of the sounds of two tuning forks with frequencies $f_1 = 2000\,\mathrm{Hz}$ and $f_2$, noting an intensity maximum every $0.5\,\mathrm{s}$. If $f_2$ is increased by $1\,\mathrm{Hz}$, the time between two successive zeros of the intensity increases. The frequency $f_2$ is:

(a) $2\,\mathrm{Hz}$ (b) $1998\,\mathrm{Hz}$ (c) $2000\,\mathrm{Hz}$ (d) $2002\,\mathrm{Hz}$

2. On the surface of a liquid at rest, interference phenomena are observed from waves coming from the synchronous sources $\mathrm{O_1}$ and $\mathrm{O_2}$. Let the circle $(\mathrm{O_1}, R)$ intersect the half-line $\mathrm{O_2}\varepsilon$ at the points A and B, which are points of constructive interference, while between A and B there is one more such point. The distance AB is equal to:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2019-1-fig1.png

(a) $\lambda$ (b) $2\lambda$ (c) $3\lambda$ (d) $4\lambda$

3. In the transmission system of a bicycle, the radii of the front and the rear gear are in the ratio $\dfrac{R_1}{R_2} = \dfrac{3}{1}$, while those of the rear gear and the wheel are in the ratio $\dfrac{R_2}{R_3} = \dfrac{1}{10}$. If the pedals rotate with frequency $2\,\mathrm{Hz}$, the radius of the rear gear is $3\,\mathrm{cm}$ and the wheels roll without slipping, then the speed of the bicycle is:

(a) $3.6\pi\,\mathrm{m/s}$ (b) $7.2\pi\,\mathrm{m/s}$ (c) $10.8\pi\,\mathrm{m/s}$ (d) $14.4\pi\,\mathrm{m/s}$

4. A small body is placed, and is in equilibrium, on the free upper end of a spring whose lower end is fixed at the base of a smooth inclined plane. The spring is compressed by $8\,\mathrm{cm}$. A second, identical body is placed in contact with the first. Until their first instantaneous stop, they will have travelled on the inclined plane a distance:

(a) $4\,\mathrm{cm}$ (b) $8\,\mathrm{cm}$ (c) $12\,\mathrm{cm}$ (d) $16\,\mathrm{cm}$

5. A U-shaped tube, open to the air at both ends, contains mercury. Water is poured into the left arm so that a water column of height H is formed. If the densities of water and mercury are $\rho_{\nu\varepsilon\rho}$ and $\rho_{\upsilon\delta\rho}$ respectively, the height above its initial level to which the mercury rises in the right arm is:

(a) $\mathrm{H}\cdot\dfrac{\rho_{\nu\varepsilon\rho}}{\rho_{\upsilon\delta\rho}}$ (b) $\dfrac{\mathrm{H}}{2}\cdot\dfrac{\rho_{\upsilon\delta\rho}}{\rho_{\nu\varepsilon\rho}}$ (c) $\dfrac{\mathrm{H}}{2}\cdot\dfrac{\rho_{\nu\varepsilon\rho}}{\rho_{\upsilon\delta\rho}}$ (d) $2\mathrm{H}\cdot\dfrac{\rho_{\nu\varepsilon\rho}}{\rho_{\upsilon\delta\rho}}$

6. Three spheres A, B, Γ of equal size and with masses $m$, $3m$, $4m$ respectively are at rest on a smooth horizontal plane, with B between A and Γ. Sphere A is launched with a velocity of magnitude $\upsilon$ towards sphere Γ. If all collisions are central and elastic, the total number of collisions that will take place is:

(a) 1 (b) 2 (c) 3 (d) 4

7. If the point K, in the snapshot of the figure, has a vertically downward velocity while P is at rest, the wave is:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2019-1-fig2.png

(a) standing

(b) travelling towards the right

(c) travelling towards the left

(d) the data are not sufficient for us to know

8. A body performs SHM with amplitude A. At the instants when the displacement from the equilibrium position is $\dfrac{\sqrt{5}}{3}\mathrm{A}$, the ratio $\dfrac{U}{K}$ of the potential to the kinetic energy of the oscillation has a value equal to:

(a) $\dfrac{5}{3}$ (b) $\dfrac{9}{5}$ (c) $\dfrac{5}{4}$ (d) $\dfrac{5}{9}$

9. A wheel rolls without slipping on a horizontal terrace and, on reaching its edge, leaves it and falls. Considering the air resistance negligible, during the fall and until it reaches the ground the velocity of its lowest point has direction:

(a) vertically downwards

(b) horizontal, in the sense of the initial motion

(c) horizontal, opposite to the sense of the initial motion

(d) oblique

10. Two synchronous sources $\mathrm{O_1}$ and $\mathrm{O_2}$, a distance $(\mathrm{O_1O_2}) = 10\,\mathrm{m}$ apart, produce waves on the surface of water, and interference phenomena are observed. The equation of oscillation of a point B of the straight segment $\mathrm{O_1O_2}$, which is the one closest to the midpoint M of $\mathrm{O_1O_2}$ that oscillates with maximum amplitude, is $y = -0.2\sin 2\pi(2t-2)$ (SI). The propagation speed of the wave is:

(a) $4\,\mathrm{m/s}$ (b) $5\,\mathrm{m/s}$ (c) $2\,\mathrm{m/s}$ (d) $3\,\mathrm{m/s}$

11. A homogeneous sphere rolls without slipping with a velocity of magnitude $\upsilon_{cm}$ on a smooth horizontal plane. At some instant it collides elastically with a smooth vertical wall and returns. The magnitude of the velocity of the lowest point of the sphere after the collision is:

(a) 0 (b) $\upsilon_{cm}$ (c) $2\upsilon_{cm}$ (d) $\sqrt{2}\,\upsilon_{cm}$

12. A material point performing SHM of period T and amplitude A covers a distance S in a time interval $\dfrac{T}{4}$. The maximum value of the distance ($S_{max}$) during the above time interval is:

(a) A (b) $\sqrt{2}\,\mathrm{A}$ (c) $2\mathrm{A}$ (d) $(2-\sqrt{2})\mathrm{A}$

The force F exerted on the container because of the liquid flowing out is equal to:

(a) $\dfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{PA}$ (b) $\mathrm{PA}$ (c) $\dfrac{3}{2}\mathrm{PA}$ (d) $2\mathrm{PA}$

(a) $0.4\,\mathrm{m}$ (b) $0.5\,\mathrm{m}$ (c) $0.8\,\mathrm{m}$ (d) $1\,\mathrm{m}$

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2019-1-fig3.png

(a) $p_A = p_{\alpha\tau\mu}$ (b) $p_A = p_{\alpha\tau\mu} + \rho g h$ (c) $p_A = p_{\alpha\tau\mu} - \rho g h$ (d) $p_A = 0$

A sphere of mass m with a horizontal velocity of magnitude $\upsilon$ becomes embedded perpendicularly in the centre of the door. The air resistance is considered negligible and there is no friction in the axis of rotation of the door. If the moment of inertia of the door about the axis of rotation is $I = \dfrac{1}{3}ML^2$, the time it will need to close is:

(a) $\dfrac{\pi L(4M+3m)}{12m\upsilon}$ (b) $\dfrac{L(4M+3m)}{m\upsilon}$ (c) $\dfrac{\pi L}{2m\upsilon}\left(\dfrac{M}{3}+\dfrac{m}{4}\right)$ (d) $\dfrac{\pi L(4M+3m)}{2m\upsilon}$

From the superposition of the original and the reflected pulse, which has the higher frequency, beats of frequency $100\,\mathrm{Hz}$ are produced. If the speed of the ultrasound in the body amounts to $1540\,\mathrm{m/s}$, then the maximum speed of oscillation of the surface of the heart is:

(a) $2.57\,\mathrm{cm/s}$ (b) $2.57\,\mathrm{mm/s}$ (c) $25.7\,\mathrm{cm/s}$ (d) $0.257\,\mathrm{mm/s}$

18. On the surface of an elastic medium there are two identical wave sources, which start their oscillation simultaneously, producing waves of wavelength $\lambda$. At a point K of the elastic medium the two waves arrive, one wave having travelled a distance greater than the other by $\dfrac{5}{4}\lambda$, and they interfere with amplitude $\mathrm{A_1}$. We decrease the oscillation frequency of the sources by $\dfrac{1}{3}$ relative to the initial one, without changing their amplitude, and then the amplitude of oscillation of point K becomes $\mathrm{A_2}$. The ratio $\dfrac{\mathrm{A_1}}{\mathrm{A_2}}$ is equal to:

(a) 1 (b) $\dfrac{1}{2}$ (c) $\sqrt{\dfrac{3}{2}}$ (d) $\sqrt{\dfrac{2}{3}}$

19. A thin rod OA, of mass M and length L, is hinged at its end O and is kept horizontal, suspended by a vertical string at the position B, where $(\mathrm{OB}) = x$. When the string is cut, the force from the hinge instantaneously does not change.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2019-1-fig4.png

If the moment of inertia of the rod about an axis passing through its midpoint and perpendicular to it is $I_{cm} = \dfrac{1}{12}ML^2$, then the distance x is equal to:

(a) $\dfrac{L}{2}$ (b) $\dfrac{2L}{3}$ (c) $\dfrac{3L}{4}$ (d) $\dfrac{L}{4}$

20. At the middle of a long, homogeneous, smooth plank a small body is placed at rest, and the system is in equilibrium horizontally, resting on a fixed support located below the plank, exactly at its middle. An explosion releases the two unequal pieces into which the body splits, and they begin to slide without friction along the length of the plank. The plank then:

(a) will tilt towards the side of the larger mass

(b) will tilt towards the side of the smaller mass

(c) will continue to be in equilibrium in the horizontal position

(d) will perform an oscillation

problems.title: Problem B
problems.problem:
Problem B

The scooter of the figure consists of a body and two identical wheels. The wheels are considered cylinders (not necessarily homogeneous) which rotate, without friction, about massless axles that are fitted to the body.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2019-2-fig1.png

[Labels in the figure: πλάγια όψη = side view; κάτοψη = top view.]

The axles are perpendicular to the wheels and pass through the centres of the wheels, which are also their centres of mass. The front axle is $12\,\mathrm{cm}$ from the centre of mass of the body, while the rear axle is $8\,\mathrm{cm}$ from the centre of mass of the body. Each wheel has mass $m = 0.5\,\mathrm{kg}$ and radius $R = 0.05\,\mathrm{m}$.

For the moment of inertia of the wheels, about the axles mentioned above, accept that $I = \lambda m R^2$, where $\lambda$ is a positive number.

problems.title: Problem C. Experimental part
problems.problem:
Problem C. Experimental part

To measure time with the greatest accuracy we use digital timers that are triggered by special infrared-radiation sensors, the photogates. With these, and with the help of different modes of their operation, we can directly measure the times over which experimental processes evolve and indirectly calculate other physical quantities (such as time intervals, average velocity, instantaneous velocity, acceleration, etc.).

From the top of an inclined plane (Figure 1) a homogeneous cylindrical body of radius r is left to roll, without initial velocity. Let $\upsilon_{cm1}$ and $\upsilon_{cm2}$ be the velocities of the centre of mass of the body at the positions where the two photogates are located; the photogates are a distance $d = S_2 - S_1$ apart, as in the following figure.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2019-3-fig1.png

Figure 1. The experimental arrangement

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2019-3-fig2.png

Figure 2. The calculation of Δt

[Labels in the figures: φωτοπύλη 1, 2 = photogate 1, 2; Αρχική θέση κυλιόμενου σώματος = initial position of the rolling body; αρχή μέτρησης = start of measurement; τέλος μέτρησης = end of measurement.]

For the motion of the body from the first photogate to the second, the following relations hold:

$$\frac{1}{2}m\upsilon_{cm1}^2 + \frac{1}{2}I\omega_1^2 + mgh = \frac{1}{2}m\upsilon_{cm2}^2 + \frac{1}{2}I\omega_2^2 \quad (1)$$

$\upsilon_{cm1} = \omega_1 . r$ (2), $\upsilon_{cm2} = \omega_2 . r$ (3), $\upsilon_{cm2} = \upsilon_{cm1} + \alpha_{cm} . \Delta t$ (4), $d = \upsilon_{cm1} . \Delta t + \dfrac{1}{2}\alpha_{cm} . \Delta t^2$ (5)

By eliminating $\Delta t$ (the measurement of the time interval $\Delta t$ is achieved with the help of a system of 2 photogates and an electronic timer, and the time interval of the motion of the body from the first photogate to the second photogate, which is a distance d away, is calculated directly each time (see also Figure 2)) between equations (4) and (5), it follows that: $\upsilon_{cm2}^2 - \upsilon_{cm1}^2 = 2\alpha_{cm} . d$ (6)

From relations (1), (2), (3) and (6) the relation $\alpha_{cm} . d\left(1+\dfrac{I}{mr^2}\right) = g . h$ (7) follows,

so that $\alpha_{cm} = \dfrac{g}{\left(1+\dfrac{I}{mr^2}\right) . d} . h$ (8)

From relation (8) we find that the acceleration of the centre of mass of the rolling body is proportional to the vertical distance between the two positions of the body (i.e. of the 2 photogates). The graph of the function $\alpha_{cm} = f(h)$ is a straight line (Figure 3).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2019-3-fig3.png

Figure 3. The graph $\alpha_{cm} = f(h)$

If we define as $K = \dfrac{g}{\left(1+\dfrac{I}{mr^2}\right)d}$ the slope of $\alpha_{cm} = f(h)$, then by solving the last relation for I it follows that: $I = mr^2\left(\dfrac{g}{K . d} - 1\right)$ (9)

That is, for certain values of h we must calculate the corresponding values of the acceleration of the centre of mass of the cylinder and construct the graph of $\alpha_{cm} = f(h)$.

The difference in height (h) between the two photogates is calculated from the formula $h = d . \dfrac{H}{L}$ (since $\sin\varphi = \dfrac{h}{d} = \dfrac{H}{L}$, or because of the similarity of triangles), where: $d = S_2 - S_1$ is the distance between the photogates along the inclined plane, $L = 0.365\,\mathrm{m}$ is the total length of the inclined plane and H is the reading of the electronic distance meter for each position of the inclined plane, after the reference plane has first been made horizontal (with a spirit level) ($H = 0$).

To calculate the acceleration of the centre of mass of the cylinder, we take $t = 0$ to be the instant at which we release the body from the top of the inclined plane without initial velocity, $t_1$ the instant at which the body passes through the first photogate, having been displaced from its initial position by $S_1$, and $t_2$ the instant at which the body passes through the second photogate, having been displaced from the top of the inclined plane by $S_2$. For $S_1$ and $S_2$ the following relations hold:

$S_1 = \dfrac{1}{2}\alpha_{cm}t_1^2$ (10)

$S_2 = \dfrac{1}{2}\alpha_{cm}t_2^2$ (11)

We solve relations (10) and (11) for $t_1$, $t_2$, subtract them side by side, and the relation $\Delta t = t_2 - t_1 = \sqrt{\dfrac{2}{\alpha_{cm}}} . \left(\sqrt{S_2} - \sqrt{S_1}\right)$ follows, from which the final relation is easily deduced:

$\alpha_{cm} = \dfrac{2}{\Delta t^2}\left(\sqrt{S_2} - \sqrt{S_1}\right)^2$ (12)

Required apparatus:

Multi-purpose inclined-plane apparatus, electronic distance meter.

Electronic timer and accessories (photogates, power supply).

Metal cylinder of diameter $10\,\mathrm{mm}$.

Electronic balance, distance meter, vernier caliper, spirit level.

EXPERIMENTAL PROCEDURE

First we measured the mass and the radius of the cylinder and recorded the values in the table below (given to you). We placed the two photogates on the plane. With the spirit level we found the position at which the inclined plane is horizontal and we zeroed the electronic distance meter ($H = 0$).

We measured the distance of the photogates from the top of the inclined plane and recorded the values $S_1$, $S_2$ in the Table of the answer sheet.

We activated the electronic timer in the appropriate measurement mode (when the body passes through the photogates the timer will record the time interval $\Delta t$ of the motion from the first photogate to the second (Figure 2)).

We then raised the inclined plane by a small amount H and recorded the value of the electronic distance meter in the table below.

We let the cylinder roll from the top of the inclined plane and recorded the reading of the electronic timer in the table below.

We repeated the measurement for five different inclinations of the inclined plane in total and recorded the readings of the distance meter (H) and of the timer ($\Delta t$) in the Table of the answer sheet.

[Table of the answer sheet (page 2 of the answer sheet), with the values as printed:]

$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline m\ (\mathrm{kg}) & r\ (\mathrm{m}) & S_1\ (\mathrm{m}) & S_2\ (\mathrm{m}) & d = S_2 - S_1\ (\mathrm{m}) & L\ (\mathrm{m}) \\ \hline 0.0426 & 0.005 & 0.10 & 0.25 & 0.15 & 0.365 \\ \hline \end{array}$$

$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline \text{No.} & H\ (\mathrm{m}) & h = d.\dfrac{H}{L}\ (\mathrm{m}) & \Delta t\ (\mathrm{s}) & \alpha_{cm} = \dfrac{2}{\Delta t^2}.\left(\sqrt{S_2}-\sqrt{S_1}\right)^2\ (\mathrm{m/s^2}) \\ \hline 1 & 0.01 & 0.00411 & 0.6996 & 0.138 \\ \hline 2 & 0.02 & & 0.4522 & \\ \hline 3 & 0.03 & & 0.3710 & \\ \hline 4 & 0.04 & & 0.3136 & \\ \hline 5 & 0.05 & & 0.2822 & \\ \hline \end{array}$$

$$\begin{array}{|l|c|} \hline \text{Slope of the graph } K & \\ \hline I_{cm,\pi\varepsilon\iota\rho} = m.r^2.\left(\dfrac{g}{d.K} - 1\right)\ (\mathrm{kg.m^2}) & \\ \hline I_{cm,\theta\varepsilon\omega\rho} = \dfrac{1}{2}mr^2\ (\mathrm{kg.m^2}) & \\ \hline \text{Relative error } \sigma = \dfrac{\left|I_{\theta\varepsilon\omega\rho} - I_{\pi\varepsilon\iota\rho}\right|}{I_{\theta\varepsilon\omega\rho}}.100\% & \\ \hline \end{array}$$

1. Calculate the value of the acceleration (to an accuracy of 3 decimal digits) with the help of relation (12) and fill in the appropriate column in the Table of the answer sheet.

2. Using the relation given to you, also fill in the column h of the Table of the answer sheet (to an accuracy of 5 decimal digits).

3. Draw on the mm paper of the answer sheet the graph of the function $\alpha_{cm} = f(h)$ from the values of the table that you filled in.

4. From the position of the 5 points on the graph, calculate the slope K of the straight line of the graph and, from relation (9), also calculate the experimental value of the moment of inertia of the cylinder (take $g = 9.81\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$).

5. Calculate the theoretical value of the moment of inertia of the cylinder and the relative error with the help of the relation: $\sigma = \dfrac{\left|I_{\theta\varepsilon\omega\rho} - I_{\pi\varepsilon\iota\rho}\right|}{I_{\theta\varepsilon\omega\rho}}.100\%$

6. Explain what the error in the above experiment may be due to, and also the reason why rather small values (1 to 5 cm) were chosen as the values of H.

7. Do you think that we could measure the $I_{cm}$ of a battery or of a half-full cylindrical container of air freshener with the above experimental procedure?

8. What changes would you make, both in the experimental procedure and in the calculation of the relative error, if you were measuring the $I_{cm}$ of a cylindrical shell?

problems.title: Problem D. Experimental part
problems.problem:
Problem D. Experimental part

Introduction

Reformulating the fundamental law of mechanics $F = m\cdot a$ we are easily led to the generalised form of Newton's 2nd Law:

$$F = \frac{p_{\text{τελ}} - p_{\text{αρχ}}}{\Delta t} \qquad (1)$$

According to this relation, for the momentum of a body to change, a force must be exerted. Solving (1) for the product $F\cdot\Delta t$ we have:

$$F\cdot\Delta t = p_{\text{τελ}} - p_{\text{αρχ}} \quad \text{or} \quad F\cdot\Delta t = \Delta p \quad \text{or} \quad J = \Delta p \qquad (2)$$

The new physical quantity $J$, which for a constant force is equal to the product of the force exerted on the body times the total time of application, $F\cdot\Delta t$, is called the "impulse" of the force and is equivalent to the change of the momentum of the body on which the force acts for some time interval. If the force exerted on the body is not constant but variable, the impulse is calculated in practice from the area of the region enclosed by the function $F = f(t)$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2019-2-4-fig1.png

The impulse is a vector, has the dimensions of momentum ($\mathrm{N\cdot sec}$) and is denoted internationally by $J$. Equality (2) corresponds to the impulse–momentum theorem, which is particularly useful in solving mechanics exercises.

In order to investigate by quantitative measurements the validity of the impulse–momentum theorem, the following experiment was carried out: A body of constant mass moves in a straight line on a smooth horizontal plane, with negligible friction. At some point of its path the body meets and collides with another body which is stationary and fixed–rigidly immobile, which in this way can be considered to have infinitely large mass. The body rebounds from the obstacle because of a short-duration varying force which it receives, with the result that its momentum changes.

Experimental set-up

The experimental set-up used in the experiment is shown schematically in the figure below. It consists of a) a smooth horizontal plane, b) a trolley with wheels, c) a motion sensor (M), d) a force sensor (Δ), e) a data logger and f) a computer.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2019-2-4-fig2.png

[Figure labels: αισθητήρας κίνησης = motion sensor; αμαξίδιο = trolley; αισθητήρας δύναμης = force sensor.]

In this set-up the MultiLog data logger was used (found in the physics laboratories of most upper secondary schools), and the DB–Lab software was loaded on the computer. The collision of the trolley with the force sensor was chosen to be made alternatively in two ways: either by the impact of metal surfaces, or by inserting a spring fixed on the trolley, to increase the duration of the collision.

Measurements

After connecting the force and motion sensors to the interface, and the interface to the computer, on which the data-collection program is already running, the measurement procedure starts: the trolley is pushed momentarily by hand so that it moves on the horizontal plane towards the force sensor. The position sensor (M) records the distance of the trolley before, during and after the impact of the trolley on the force sensor (obstacle Δ). The evolution of the motion is shown on the computer screen (processed graph 1).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2019-2-4-fig3.png

Graph 1: Distance of the trolley from the position sensor (M). [Axes: Θέση x(m) = position x (m); Χρόνος t(s) = time t (s).]

The trolley collides with the force sensor, receives an impulse from it and moves in the opposite direction. The impulse of the short-duration force is recorded by the force sensor through the graph of force as a function of time (processed graph 2).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2019-2-4-fig4.png

Graph 2: Collision force as a function of time. [Axes: Δύναμη F (N) = force F (N); Χρόνος t (s) = time t (s).]

On the basis of the data of the experiment you are asked to answer the following questions:

1. From 0–1.8 s (in graph 1), is the trolley approaching or moving away from the impact point (Δ)? What is the direction of its motion from 1.8–3.7 s?

2. Using graph 1, determine the kind of motion of the trolley and calculate the speed with which it:

a. approaches,

b. moves away from (Δ).

3. If the mass of the trolley is 170 g, what is the total change of momentum due to the impact?

4. Using graph 2, calculate the magnitude of the impulse that caused this change of momentum.

5. Do the last two values coincide? If yes, what do you have to comment on the validity of the impulse–momentum theorem?

6. If not, in your opinion, for what reasons may the observed deviations be due?

7. Given that graph 1 does not change, how would the graph of force as a function of time (graph 2) change if the impact took place with a spring inserted, fixed on the trolley?

The largest value of the mass $M$ the sphere can have so that it is in equilibrium without the wedges moving is:

(a) $\dfrac{m}{1-\mu}$ (b) $\dfrac{\mu m}{1-\mu}$ (c) $\dfrac{2\mu m}{1-\mu}$

Choose the correct answer and justify it.

problems.title: Problem C
problems.problem:
Problem C

In a quarry, trucks are used that are suitable for transporting large blocks of marble, cut in cubic shape, with mass $3\cdot10^3\,\mathrm{Kg}$. These transports involve dangers, because they take place on roads inside the quarry, horizontal or inclined, and usually without the marble blocks being tied down. The drivers are experienced and trust their abilities because they know that strong static friction develops between the marble base and the surface of the truck bed, with coefficient $\mu = 0.6$. Nevertheless, your advice is needed to deal with the following unexpected situations:

A. The truck loaded with the marble block moves on a horizontal road, but the driver is forced to brake and, decelerating, brings it to rest in a time of $3\,\mathrm{s}$. Because of the deceleration there is a danger that the marble block slides forwards on the truck bed. This will happen if the deceleration exceeds a limiting (maximum) value. Draw and justify the direction of the friction force exerted by the truck bed on the marble, and then calculate the maximum speed the truck can reach so that sliding is avoided.

B. The truck then follows an uphill road with inclination $26^\circ$ ($\sin26^\circ = 0.43$ and $\cos26^\circ = 0.90$). The danger now is that the marble block slides backwards. So the driver uses the accelerator with care so as not to exceed an acceleration value $\alpha_{\max}$, which you must calculate, for the marble block to remain at rest on the truck bed.

C. At the end of its route the truck stops on a horizontal platform and its crane undertakes to unload the marble from the truck bed, which is at $h = 2.5\,\mathrm{m}$ from the ground. The marble is attached with a steel cable and the crane adjusts the force $F$ that stretches the cable, as it starts to lift the marble initially, in the way shown in the table.

$$\begin{array}{|c|c|} \hline t\ (\mathrm{s}) & F\ (\times10^3\ \mathrm{N}) \\ \hline 0.0 - 4.0 & 31.5 \\ \hline 4.0 - 6.5 & 27.6 \\ \hline \geq 6.5 & 28.5 \\ \hline \end{array}$$

While the lifting lasts, the arm of the crane rotates slightly so that the marble is deposited on the surface of the ground.

You are asked to study, with position–time (x–t) and velocity–time (υ–t) equations, the three stages of this procedure and to represent graphically the algebraic value of the velocity as a function of time.

problems.title: Problem D. Experimental part
problems.problem:
Problem D. Experimental part

When a body starts moving in a straight line from position $x = 0$, at the instant $t = 0$, with constant acceleration $\alpha$, without initial velocity, its position $x$ and its velocity $\upsilon$ at every instant $t$ are determined by the equations: $x = \dfrac{1}{2}\alpha t^2$ and $\upsilon = \alpha t$.

From these equations the relation $\upsilon^2 = 2\alpha x$ (1) follows.

From equation (1) we observe that the square of the velocity ($\upsilon^2$) of the moving body is proportional to its corresponding position ($x$). Therefore the graph $\upsilon^2$–$x$ is a straight line passing through the origin of the axes, and the slope of this line is equal to twice the acceleration of the motion of the body.

On the basis of these observations, we can examine experimentally whether the motion of a trolley that starts from rest is uniformly accelerated, and calculate its acceleration from the corresponding experimental graph $\upsilon^2$–$x$.

To draw the experimental graph $\upsilon^2$–$x$, we must be able to measure the velocity of the trolley at various positions through which it passes during its motion. This measurement is achieved with the help of a photogate – electronic timer system.

Required instruments:

1. Laboratory trolley ($M = 0.565\,\mathrm{Kg}$)

2. Pulley, string, weight ($m = 100\,\mathrm{g}$)

3. An electronic timer with a photogate

4. Electronic balance

5. A paper strip of width $\Delta x = 1\,\mathrm{cm}$

6. Ruler or measuring tape

EXPERIMENTAL PROCEDURE

We assemble the experimental set-up shown in the figure.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2019-3-4-fig1.png

[Figure labels: χάρτινη ταινία = paper strip; Φωτοπύλη = photogate.]

We consider friction negligible and the pulley weightless. Therefore we do not take its rotation into account, and consequently the tensions of the string on the two bodies of masses $M$ and $m$ respectively will be equal to each other.

Also, the two bodies will accelerate (with the string taut) with accelerations of equal magnitude, as shown in the figure.

The acceleration with which the bodies will move is given by the relation: $\alpha_{\text{θεωρ}} = \dfrac{mg}{m+M}$ (2).

On the trolley we have stuck a small paper strip of width $\Delta x = 1\,\mathrm{cm}$, perpendicular to the direction of its motion and of suitable length, so that passing through the photogate it interrupts its light (infrared) beam. To measure time with maximum accuracy we use digital timers that are triggered by special sensors of infrared radiation, the photogates. With these, and with the help of different modes of operation, we can directly measure the times over which experimental processes evolve and indirectly calculate other physical quantities (such as average velocity, instantaneous velocity, acceleration, force, etc.).

We activate the electronic timer in the mode in which it measures the time $\Delta t$ (of passage) from the beginning of the shading of the photogate by the paper strip until the end of the shading, i.e. the time interval of motion of the trolley over a distance $\Delta x$ equal to the width of the paper strip. The average velocity of each trolley can be calculated from the relation $\upsilon = \dfrac{\Delta x}{\Delta t}$, where $\Delta x$ is the displacement of the trolley that takes place in time $\Delta t$, or alternatively where $\Delta t$ is the time required for the paper strip of width $\Delta x$ to pass through the photogate. For very small time intervals $\Delta t$ we accept that the average velocity is identical with the instantaneous velocity of the trolley.

1) We place the photogate at a distance of $0.1\,\mathrm{m}$ from the starting position of the trolley.

2) We weigh the masses $M$ and $m$ of the trolley and the weight respectively.

3) We let the trolley free to move and record the passage time $\Delta t$ of the paper strip in the table below. We repeat the measurement three times (for the same position of the photogate) and find the mean value of the passage time $\langle\Delta t\rangle$, which we record in the table below (it is given to you).

4) We then place the photogate successively at distances $0.2\,\mathrm{m}$, $0.3\,\mathrm{m}$, $0.4\,\mathrm{m}$, $0.5\,\mathrm{m}$, $0.6\,\mathrm{m}$ and $0.7\,\mathrm{m}$ from the starting position of the trolley and repeat step 3, completing the table.

$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline x\ (\mathrm{m}) & \Delta t\ (\mathrm{s}) & \langle\Delta t\rangle\ (\mathrm{s}) & \Delta x\ (\mathrm{m}) & \upsilon = \Delta x/\langle\Delta t\rangle & \upsilon^2\ (\mathrm{m^2/s^2}) \\ & & \text{mean value} & \text{of strip} & (\mathrm{m/s}) & \\ \hline 0.1 & 0.0213,\ 0.0214,\ 0.0216 & 0.02143 & 0.01 & & \\ \hline 0.2 & 0.0155,\ 0.0153,\ 0.0154 & 0.01540 & 0.01 & & \\ \hline 0.3 & 0.0128,\ 0.0125,\ 0.0127 & 0.01267 & 0.01 & & \\ \hline 0.4 & 0.0109,\ 0.0108,\ 0.0108 & 0.01083 & 0.01 & & \\ \hline 0.5 & 0.0098,\ 0.0097,\ 0.0097 & 0.00973 & 0.01 & & \\ \hline 0.6 & 0.0088,\ 0.0089,\ 0.0088 & 0.00883 & 0.01 & & \\ \hline 0.7 & 0.0083,\ 0.0082,\ 0.0083 & 0.00827 & 0.01 & & \\ \hline \end{array}$$

1. Prove the relations $\upsilon^2 = 2\alpha x$ (1) and $\alpha_{\text{θεωρ}} = \dfrac{mg}{m+M}$ (2).

2. For each trolley–photogate distance, calculate the velocity $\upsilon$ and the square of the velocity $\upsilon^2$, completing the corresponding columns in the table above (on the answer sheet you were given).

3. Draw the graph of the square of the velocity as a function of the distance ($\upsilon^2$–$x$) on the mm graph paper.

4. From the slope of the line, calculate the experimental value $\alpha_{\text{πειρ}}$ of the acceleration of the trolley.

5. From the theoretical relation (2), calculate the theoretical value of the acceleration $\alpha_{\text{θεωρ}}$ of the trolley (take $g = 9.81\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$).

6. Calculate the relative error with the help of the relation: $\sigma = \dfrac{\left|\alpha_{\text{θεωρ}} - \alpha_{\text{πειρ}}\right|}{\alpha_{\text{θεωρ}}}\cdot100\%$

7. Explain the possible reasons why the value of the relative error $\sigma$ has the value you estimated.

problems.title: Problem D. Experimental problem: study of the SHM of a mass–spring system
problems.problem:
Problem D. Experimental problem: study of the SHM of a mass–spring system

FIELD OF INVESTIGATION:

1. Excitation of a mass–spring system to perform SHM.

2. Investigation of the relation between the characteristic quantities of the oscillating system and those of SHM.

3. Taking measurements in order to calculate the value of the spring constant k and of the mass $m_\varepsilon$ of the spring, and to verify the validity of the principle of conservation of energy.

PREREQUISITE KNOWLEDGE:

A uniform metal cylinder of mass m attached to the free end of a spring can be set in motion after an additional extension or compression of the spring is produced; the spring is suspended from a fixed point with its axis vertical.

Ignoring every other force except the weight of the body and the elastic force of the spring, we can show that the motion of the body is described by the equation $x(t) = \mathrm{A}\sin(\omega t + \varphi)$ (1), which also identifies the motion as SHM with angular frequency ω and period

$$T = 2\cdot\pi\cdot\sqrt{\dfrac{m}{K}} \qquad (2)$$

The periodicity of SHM is ensured by the fact that when the time is increased by $\dfrac{2\cdot\lambda\cdot\pi}{\omega}$ (λ a natural number), (1) does not change form, since:

$x\left(t + \dfrac{2\lambda\pi}{\omega}\right) = \mathrm{A}\sin\left\{\omega\left(t + \dfrac{2\lambda\pi}{\omega}\right) + \varphi\right\} = \mathrm{A}\sin(\omega t + 2\lambda\pi + \varphi) = \mathrm{A}\sin(\omega t + \varphi)$.

Relation (2) holds in the case of a massless spring (ideal spring). In practice, however, and as a rule, the mass of the spring $m_\varepsilon$ is of the same order of magnitude as the mass m of the body, so if it is not ignored it will appear in the expression for the period.

It can be shown that: $T = 2\cdot\pi\cdot\sqrt{\dfrac{m + \dfrac{m_\varepsilon}{3}}{k}}$ or $T^2 = \dfrac{4\cdot\pi^2}{k}\cdot m + \dfrac{4\cdot\pi^2}{3\cdot k}\cdot m_\varepsilon$, i.e. the equation $T^2 = f(m)$ is linear, of the form $\mathbf{T^2 = a.m + b}$, if we set $\mathbf{a} = \dfrac{\mathbf{4\pi^2}}{\mathbf{k}}$ (slope of the straight line) and $\mathbf{b} = \dfrac{\mathbf{4\pi^2}}{\mathbf{3k}}\,\mathbf{m_\varepsilon}$ (point of intersection with the $T^2$ axis).

We can therefore measure the period T of the oscillations of the system for different values of the mass m and, from the graph, calculate the values of the characteristics k and $m_\varepsilon$ of the spring.

EXPERIMENTAL PART

We experiment with an arrangement that includes a vertical spring suspended from a fixed point, with the possibility of hanging different masses on its free end. When the system is excited, and for a short time interval it is considered to perform SHM, the position of the mass as it moves along the vertical axis can be detected by a transmitter–position (distance) sensor placed below the mass, on the axis of its motion.

The transmitter locates the position x of the oscillating mass at every instant t and sends the data to a computer, where, after their collection and analysis by special software, the graph $x = f(t) = \mathrm{A}\sin(\omega t + \varphi)$ is displayed.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2021-4-fig1.jpg

Each time a different mass m is used, which is set into SHM of amplitude about $20\,\mathrm{cm}$, so that from the corresponding graph the period is calculated as the time difference $t_2 - t_1$ between two successive peaks of the x–t curve.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2021-4-fig2.png

Image 1: m = 0.4 Kg

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2021-4-fig3.png

Image 2: m = 0.5 Kg

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2021-4-fig4.png

Image 3: m = 0.6 Kg

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2021-4-fig5.png

Image 4: m = 0.7 Kg

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2021-4-fig6.png

Image 5: m = 0.8 Kg

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2021-4-fig7.png

Image 6: m = 0.9 Kg

The results are recorded in Table «A»:

TABLE «A»

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c} \text{No.} & m\ (\mathrm{Kg}) & t_1\ (\mathrm{s}) & t_2\ (\mathrm{s}) & T = t_2 - t_1\ (\mathrm{s}) & T^2\ (\mathrm{s^2}) \\ \hline 1. & 0.4 & & & & \\ 2. & 0.5 & & & & \\ 3. & 0.6 & & & & \\ 4. & 0.7 & & & & \\ 5. & 0.8 & & & & \\ 6. & 0.9 & & & & \end{array}$$

D1. Calculate the period T that corresponds to each mass and its square $T^2$ (the period T to be calculated to two significant figures and $T^2$ to four).

D2. Draw the graph $T^2 = f(m)$. What is its shape and why? Find its slope a and from it calculate the spring constant k of the spring.

D3. If the theoretical value of the spring constant is $k = 25\,\mathrm{N/m}$, calculate the absolute error Δk and the relative error (Δk)% of the measurement.

D4. From the graph, determine the point of intersection of the graph with the $T^2$ axis and from the value of b calculate the mass $m_\varepsilon$ of the spring.

D5. If the mass of the spring was determined by weighing to be $m_\varepsilon = 300\,\mathrm{g}$, calculate the absolute error $\Delta m_\varepsilon$ and the relative error $(\Delta m_\varepsilon)\%$ of the measurement.

D6. With the method of «least squares», the determination of the coefficients a and b of the linear equation $T^2 = f(m)$ is attempted in a more accurate way than that of the approximate drawing of the graph. This is achieved from the sums in the last row of Table «B», which you will fill in. Given:

$$\alpha' = \dfrac{\mathrm{N}\cdot\sum m\cdot T^2 - \sum m\cdot\sum T^2}{N\cdot\sum m^2 - \left(\sum m\right)^2} \qquad b' = \dfrac{\sum m^2\cdot\sum T^2 - \sum (T^2\cdot m)\cdot\sum m}{N\cdot\sum m^2 - \left(\sum m\right)^2}$$

TABLE «B»

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c} \text{No.} & m\ (\mathrm{Kg}) & T^2\ (\mathrm{s^2}) & m^2\ (\mathrm{kg^2}) & T^2\cdot m\ (\mathrm{kg\cdot s^2}) \\ \hline 1. & 0.4 & & & \\ 2. & 0.5 & & & \\ 3. & 0.6 & & & \\ 4. & 0.7 & & & \\ 5. & 0.8 & & & \\ 6. & 0.9 & & & \\ \hline \text{TOTALS} & \sum m_i = & \sum m_i^2 = & \sum T_i^2 = & \sum (T_i^2\cdot m_i) \end{array}$$

D7. From the values of the coefficients a΄ and b΄, calculate the spring constant k and the mass $m_\varepsilon$ of the spring, as well as the corresponding values of the absolute and relative errors with respect to their theoretical values.

[4+4+4+4+4+5+5 marks]

Problem C

Our effort to understand the world in which we live has led us to realise that the exploration of the microcosm is important. From the atoms of Democritus to today's elementary particles, the road passes through the construction of large accelerators (initially linear and then circular) at large research centres. One of these centres is the European CERN, which was created in 1954, with Greece being one of the 12 founding countries.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2021-2-3-fig1.jpg

The entrance of Alice, one of the experiments carried out at CERN.

A charged particle $(\Sigma_1)$ of mass $m_1 = 2\cdot10^{-16}\,\mathrm{kg}$ performs uniform circular motion with speed $\upsilon_0 = 1000\,\mathrm{km/s}$ in an accelerator $(\mathrm{E}_1)$ of radius $R_1 = 100\,\mathrm{m}$.

problems.title: Problem D. Study of the characteristic curve of an electrical source
problems.problem:
Problem D. Study of the characteristic curve of an electrical source

FIELD OF INVESTIGATION:

1. Handling simple electric circuits and taking measurements with an ammeter and a voltmeter.

2. Investigating the existence of a linear relation between the terminal voltage of an electrical source and the current flowing through it. Calculating the internal resistance of the source.

PREREQUISITE KNOWLEDGE:

The electrical source (usually we mean a battery) is used to supply electrical energy to a circuit by converting the chemical energy it contains by construction.

The potential difference between the positive and the negative terminal of the electrical source when the circuit is open, so that no electric current flows, is called the electromotive force (emf) of the source, is denoted by E and is a constructional characteristic of it.

When the electrical source is connected to an electric circuit, the electrical energy it supplies is converted into other forms of energy (e.g. thermal in a resistor, light in a lamp, kinetic in a motor, etc.) and the potential difference between its terminals is given by the relation $V = E - I\cdot r$, where $r$ is its internal resistance, which is due to the obstacles that the electric charges meet as they pass through the interior of the source.

By changing the characteristics of the loads (ohmic resistors, lamps, crystal diode) in the circuit, we are able to measure each time the current I (independent variable) and the voltage V at the terminals of the source (dependent variable). The characteristic curve $V = f(I)$ of the electrical source is the graph of the equation $V = E - I\cdot r$.

EXPERIMENTAL PART:

V–I CHARACTERISTIC CURVE OF AN ELECTRICAL SOURCE

D1. We connect the ideal voltmeter directly across the terminals of a free electrical source (battery) marked 12 V. What is its reading? What is the relation between the reading V of the voltmeter and the emf E of the electrical source, and why?

D2. We set up a series circuit that includes the electrical source, a switch, an ammeter and a “box” K, which can contain one or two or three identical resistors, of resistance $R = 24\,\Omega$ each, connected in all possible ways among themselves. Draw the basic circuit with the box.

D3. Draw all the possible combinations of the resistors inside the box and number them consecutively from 1, from the largest total resistance to the smallest.

D4. We close the switch and record in a table the readings of the ammeter (I) and of a voltmeter (V) connected to the terminals of the source. We take one pair of readings for each combination. Below you are given table (A), to which you must add, for each pair of readings, the experimental value of the resistance of the contents of box K as well as the corresponding combination of the resistors in it.

TABLE A

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c} V\ (\mathrm{V}) & 10.8 & 10.3 & 9.8 & 9.0 & 8.0 & 7.2 & 6.0 \\ \hline I\ (\mathrm{A}) & 0.15 & 0.22 & 0.27 & 0.38 & 0.50 & 0.60 & 0.75 \\ \hline R_{o\lambda}\ (\Omega)\ \text{exper.} & & & & & & & \\ \hline \text{Combination no.} & & & & & & & \\ \hline R_{o\lambda}\ (\Omega)\ \text{theor.} & & & & & & & \end{array}$$

D5. Plot on a V–I system of axes the pairs of measurements of the table and draw the most accurate line that satisfies all the measurements.

D6. What equation does the graph you drew represent, based on the experimental values, and what are the coordinates of the intersections of the graph with the axes? What would happen to the circuit if the box contained only a wire of zero resistance?

D7. Calculate from the diagram the internal resistance r of the source. What would the form of the graph $V = f(I)$ be for an ideal source with no internal resistance?

problems.title: Problem D. Study of the electromagnetic force on a current-carrying conductor
problems.problem:
Problem D. Study of the electromagnetic force on a current-carrying conductor

EXPERIMENTAL PART

THEORY

Consider a straight conductor of length L carrying an electric current I. If the conductor is placed in a magnetic field $\vec{B}$ with its direction perpendicular to the field lines, an electromagnetic force is expected to be exerted on it, as the resultant of the forces exerted by the magnetic field on the moving electric charges.

Suppose that carriers (e.g. free electrons), each with electric charge q, moving with velocity $\upsilon$, travel the length of the conductor in time Δt; then: $L = \upsilon\cdot\Delta t$ and $\sum q = I\,\Delta t$, therefore $L = \upsilon\dfrac{\sum q}{I}$ or $\sum q\cdot\upsilon = L\cdot I$ (1).

The electromagnetic (Lorentz) force exerted by a magnetic field on an electric charge moving perpendicular to its field lines is given by the relation $F = B\upsilon q$; therefore the corresponding macroscopic force on the conductor, because of (1), will have magnitude $F_L = \sum F = B\upsilon\sum q = BIL$ and is known as the Laplace force.

EXPERIMENTAL PROCEDURE

The determination of the characteristics of the Laplace force is attempted with the experimental procedure described here.

An electric circuit is set up, as shown in the figure, which includes as power supply a source of constant (DC) voltage 24 V in series with a rheostat, through which the current can be varied. Connected in series in the circuit is a straight conductor (a wire), which passes, without touching, between the poles of a horseshoe magnet placed on the pan of an electronic balance. The direction of the conductor is perpendicular to the field lines of the uniform magnetic field.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2022-4-fig1.png

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2022-4-fig2.png

Initially the circuit is open, so the reading of the balance, which is the normal force $\mathrm{N}_o$, is equal to the weight of the magnet $W_o = m_o g$, and is therefore proportional to its mass $m_o$. If we close the switch, depending on the polarity of the source and hence on the direction of the electric current in the conductor, the reading of the balance will change, showing an "apparent" weight $W$, which will be equal to the new normal force $\mathrm{N} = W_o \pm F_L'$, where $F_L'$ is the electromagnetic force exerted by the straight current-carrying conductor on the magnet. In essence, the magnitude of this force, which is added to or subtracted from the weight of the magnet, is equal to the magnitude of the force $F_L$ exerted by the magnet on the current-carrying conductor, as an action–reaction pair. The aim of the experiment is to take measurements for various values of the length of the conductor that lies inside the magnetic field and of the electric current, in order to relate the magnitude of the force $F_L$ to the length $L$ of the conductor and the current I flowing through it.

TAKING MEASUREMENTS

To simplify the calculations, let us take the directions of the field lines and of the current as in the figure, so that the magnitude of the force $F_L$ is added to the weight $W_o$ of the magnet, and therefore the reading of the balance increases. Let us note here that the balance measures force, but is calibrated so that its reading equals the mass.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2022-4-fig3.png

With the switch open we note the reading of the balance, $m_o = 260\,\mathrm{g}$, which corresponds to the weight of the magnet $W_o = m_o g = 260\cdot10^{-3}\cdot 9.81\,\mathrm{N} = 2.55\,\mathrm{N}$.

We close the switch and adjust so that the current has the value $I = 1\,\mathrm{A}$ for each value of the length of the conductor, from $1\,\mathrm{cm}$ to $10\,\mathrm{cm}$, that we choose each time to lie inside the magnetic field. For each value of this length we note the reading of the balance and record the results in Table 1:

TABLE 1

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c} \text{Conductor} & \text{Length } L\ (\mathrm{cm}) & \text{Current } I\ (\mathrm{A}) & \text{Balance reading } m\ (\mathrm{g}) \\ \hline \mathrm{L1} & 1 & 1 & 260.102 \\ \mathrm{L2} & 2 & 1 & 260.205 \\ \mathrm{L3} & 3 & 1 & 260.307 \\ \mathrm{L4} & 4 & 1 & 260.407 \\ \mathrm{L5} & 5 & 1 & 260.510 \\ \mathrm{L6} & 6 & 1 & 260.612 \\ \mathrm{L7} & 7 & 1 & 260.715 \\ \mathrm{L8} & 8 & 1 & 260.817 \\ \mathrm{L9} & 9 & 1 & 260.918 \\ \mathrm{L10} & 10 & 1 & 261.020 \end{array}$$

We repeat the measurement procedure, choosing a particular fixed length of the conductor $L = 4.0\,\mathrm{cm}$ and adjusting so that the current I takes various values from $0.2\,\mathrm{A}$ to $2\,\mathrm{A}$. For each value of the current we note the reading of the balance and record the results in Table 2:

TABLE 2

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c} \text{Conductor} & \text{Current } I\ (\mathrm{A}) & \text{Length } (\mathrm{cm}) & \text{Balance reading } (\mathrm{g}) \\ \hline \mathrm{I1} & 0.2 & 4 & 260.082 \\ \mathrm{I2} & 0.4 & 4 & 260.164 \\ \mathrm{I3} & 0.6 & 4 & 260.245 \\ \mathrm{I4} & 0.8 & 4 & 260.325 \\ \mathrm{I5} & 1.0 & 4 & 260.408 \\ \mathrm{I6} & 1.2 & 4 & 260.490 \\ \mathrm{I7} & 1.4 & 4 & 260.571 \\ \mathrm{I8} & 1.6 & 4 & 260.652 \\ \mathrm{I9} & 1.8 & 4 & 260.734 \\ \mathrm{I10} & 2.0 & 4 & 260.815 \end{array}$$

PROCESSING THE MEASUREMENTS

For each "reading" $m$ of the balance, because of equilibrium, $\mathrm{N} = W_o + F_L$ or $mg = m_o g + F_L$ or $(m - m_o)g = F_L$ or $F_L = \Delta m\cdot g$.

D1. From the measurements of Table 1, fill in the entries of Table 3. [4 marks]

TABLE 3

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c|c} \text{Conductor} & I\ (\mathrm{A}) & L\ (\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm{m}) & m_0\ (\mathrm{g}) & m\ (\mathrm{g}) & \Delta m\ (\mathrm{g}) & F_L\ (\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{N}) \\ \hline \mathrm{L1} & 1 & 1 & 260 & 260.102 & & \\ \mathrm{L2} & 1 & 2 & 260 & 260.205 & & \\ \mathrm{L3} & 1 & 3 & 260 & 260.307 & & \\ \mathrm{L4} & 1 & 4 & 260 & 260.407 & & \\ \mathrm{L5} & 1 & 5 & 260 & 260.510 & & \\ \mathrm{L6} & 1 & 6 & 260 & 260.612 & & \\ \mathrm{L7} & 1 & 7 & 260 & 260.715 & & \\ \mathrm{L8} & 1 & 8 & 260 & 260.817 & & \\ \mathrm{L9} & 1 & 9 & 260 & 260.918 & & \\ \mathrm{L10} & 1 & 10 & 260 & 261.020 & & \end{array}$$

D2. On a system of rectangular axes, plot the graph of the force (axis $y'y$) against the length $L$ of the conductor (axis $x'x$), determining the points from the data of Table 3. What is the conclusion from the shape of the graph? [3 marks]

D3. From the measurements of Table 2, fill in the entries of Table 4. [4 marks]

TABLE 4

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c|c} \text{Conductor} & I\ (\mathrm{A}) & L\ (\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm{m}) & m_0\ (\mathrm{g}) & m\ (\mathrm{g}) & \Delta m\ (\mathrm{g}) & F_L\ (\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{N}) \\ \hline \mathrm{I1} & 0.2 & 4 & 260 & 260.082 & & \\ \mathrm{I2} & 0.4 & 4 & 260 & 260.163 & & \\ \mathrm{I3} & 0.6 & 4 & 260 & 260.245 & & \\ \mathrm{I4} & 0.8 & 4 & 260 & 260.326 & & \\ \mathrm{I5} & 1.0 & 4 & 260 & 260.408 & & \\ \mathrm{I6} & 1.2 & 4 & 260 & 260.490 & & \\ \mathrm{I7} & 1.4 & 4 & 260 & 260.571 & & \\ \mathrm{I8} & 1.6 & 4 & 260 & 260.652 & & \\ \mathrm{I9} & 1.8 & 4 & 260 & 260.734 & & \\ \mathrm{I10} & 2.0 & 4 & 260 & 260.815 & & \end{array}$$

D4. On a system of rectangular axes, plot the graph of the force (axis $y'y$) against the current I flowing through the conductor (axis $x'x$), determining the points from the data of Table 4. What is the conclusion from the shape of the graph? [3 marks]

D5. How is the conclusion that follows from the previous findings formulated? [4 marks]

D6. What is expressed by the slope of each graph? [3 marks]

D7. Is it possible to calculate some quantity of the arrangement from the value of the slope? [4 marks]
