Problem B

B1. A plastic ring has mass M and radius R and is in equilibrium with its plane vertical. The ring touches two smooth vertical planes and a horizontal floor, which prevents it from rotating. A small ball of mass $m = \dfrac{M}{7}$ is launched with a horizontal velocity of magnitude $\upsilon_o$ from the lowest point of the ring and moves in a groove that the ring has on its inner side. The ball reaches the highest point of the groove without the ring losing contact with the horizontal floor. The magnitude g of the acceleration due to gravity is given.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2022-2-2-fig1.png

Calculate, in S.I. units, the values that the ratio $\dfrac{\upsilon_o^2}{Rg}$ can take.

[12 marks]

B2. A circular horizontal square has a roundabout for cars with centre at point Ο and radius $R = 120\,\mathrm{m}$. Four roads end at the roundabout at points Α, Β, Γ, Δ, which in pairs form quarter-circles. At time $t_o = 0$ a car with its headlights on, which shine along the straight line in front of the car, enters the roundabout at point Α. The car moves with speed of constant magnitude $\upsilon = 10\cdot\pi\,\mathrm{m/s}$ counterclockwise and leaves again at point Α. In the same horizontal plane as the square and outside it, on the straight line ΒΔ on the side of Δ and at a distance $(\mathrm{ΟΕ}) = 2R$, is the point Ε, where there is a thin vertical pole. Calculate the time at which the lights of the car will illuminate the pole.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2022-2-2-fig2.png

Consider the dimensions of the car small. Also consider the width of the road small compared with the radius of the roundabout.

[13 marks]

problems.title: Problem C
problems.problem:
Problem C

C1. Our solar system consists mainly of the Sun and the planets, which revolve around it in elliptical orbits. The Earth is the third planet in order from the Sun and completes one full revolution around it in 365 days. The most impressive is the sixth planet in order, Saturn, which has always been the favourite sight of astronomical observations because of the nine rings it has. The rings consist of dust and ice.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2022-2-3-fig1.jpg

Saturn and its rings

The Earth and Saturn revolve in the same sense in the same plane (in reality the orbital planes of the two planets form a small angle, which here we consider negligible). For the purposes of the exercise let us assume that the planets perform uniform circular motion about the centre of the Sun, which is at rest. The orbital radius of the Earth is $R_\Gamma = 150\,000\,000\,\mathrm{km}$ and that of Saturn is $R_\mathrm{K} = 1\,350\,000\,000\,\mathrm{km}$. At some instant the centres of the two planets and the centre of the Sun are collinear. Calculate the minimum time interval required for them to become collinear again. Assume that only the attractive gravitational force from the Sun acts on the planets.

[10 marks]

C2. Two children are playing in their room with a toy train. The rails of the railway lie on the horizontal floor and form two semicircles ΑΒ and ΓΔ of equal radius $R = 1\,\mathrm{m}$ and two straight segments ΒΓ and ΔΑ of length $(\mathrm{ΒΓ}) = (\mathrm{ΔΑ}) = 2\,\mathrm{m}$. The toy has an electric locomotive with a built-in wagon box of dimensions $(5\,\mathrm{cm}) \times (10\,\mathrm{cm}) \times (4\,\mathrm{cm})$ and mass $m_1 = 400\,\mathrm{g}$, and a carriage of mass $m_2 = 600\,\mathrm{g}$. The locomotive is at rest at the midpoint Μ of the straight segment ΒΓ and the carriage is at rest at the midpoint Κ of the straight segment ΑΔ. The children fill the box of the locomotive with sand of density $\rho = 2\cdot10^3\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}$ and at time $t_o = 0$ they switch on the electric motor of the locomotive, which then starts to move with constant speed $\upsilon = \dfrac{\pi+2}{20}\,\mathrm{m/s}$ towards point Γ. At the same time, through a small hole in its base, the box starts to lose sand, which falls onto the floor at a constant rate $\dfrac{\Delta m}{\Delta t} = 10\,\mathrm{g/s}$; this does not noticeably affect the magnitude of the velocity with which the train moves.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2022-2-3-fig2.png

C2.1. Calculate the magnitude of the resultant force exerted on the locomotive by the rails at the instant it is at the midpoint Ε of the semicircle ΓΔ. Assume that during the motion on the semicircle the component of the force exerted on the locomotive by the rails along the direction of its velocity is negligible.

C2.2. The locomotive collides plastically with the carriage, and the combined body then moves immediately after the collision with a speed of constant magnitude $\upsilon_\Sigma$. Calculate $\upsilon_\Sigma$, if during the collision we regard the locomotive–carriage system as isolated.

C2.3. The combined body continues to move with the speed of constant magnitude $\upsilon_\Sigma$, with which it reaches the midpoint Ζ of the semicircle ΑΒ. Calculate the magnitude of the change in momentum of the locomotive–box–sand system from point Ε to point Ζ.

The magnitude of the acceleration due to gravity $g = 10\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$ and $\pi = 3.14$ are given.

[5 + 5 + 5 marks]

problems.title: Problem D. Study of the characteristic curve of an electrical source – ohmic load – crystal diode
problems.problem:
Problem D. Study of the characteristic curve of an electrical source – ohmic load – crystal diode

FIELD OF INVESTIGATION:

1. Handling simple electric circuits and taking measurements with an ammeter and a voltmeter.

2. Constructing the characteristic curve $I = f(V)$ for an ohmic load and an incandescent lamp. Verification of Ohm's law.

3. Constructing the characteristic curve $I = f(V)$ for a p-n crystal diode. Determination of the direction of conduction.

PREREQUISITE KNOWLEDGE

When an electrical source is connected to an electric circuit, the electrical energy it supplies is converted into other forms of energy (e.g. thermal in a resistor, light in a lamp, kinetic in a motor, etc.).

By changing the characteristics of the loads (ohmic resistors, lamps, crystal diode) in the circuit, we are able to measure each time the current I and the voltage V across each load.

Thus, for a particular ohmic load (e.g. the wire of a heater) or for an incandescent lamp, the application of a voltage V (cause) establishes a current I (effect), so that the graph of the equation $I = f(V)$ is the characteristic curve of the load. Of particular importance is the linear form, which obeys Ohm's law $I = \dfrac{V}{R}$ and which does not hold in the case of the incandescent lamp.

The p-n crystal diode is a combination of two semiconductors of p type and n type (p ► n) which, depending on the polarity of the voltage across it, allows or blocks the passage of electric current. In forward bias, in which it conducts ($V_p > V_n$), the resistance of the diode is very small and the current increases rapidly with the applied voltage, while in reverse bias ($V_p < V_n$), in which it does not conduct, the current is minimal and the resistance of the diode very large. In each case the graph of the equation $I = f(V)$ is the characteristic curve of the crystal diode.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2022-2-4-fig1.png

(top) forward bias; (bottom) reverse bias

EXPERIMENTAL PART

D1. I–V CHARACTERISTIC OF AN OHMIC LOAD

We set up a series circuit that includes a DC power supply (0–20 V), a switch, a wire resistor from an electric heater (200 V/500 W), an ideal ammeter and an ideal voltmeter connected across the resistor.

D1.1 Draw the electric circuit. What is the reading of the ammeter when the reading of the voltmeter across the resistor is zero?

By turning the voltage regulator of the power supply, we successively increase the reading of the voltmeter by 4 V each time, up to and including 20 V, and record the pairs of V–I readings in table (A1).

TABLE A1

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c|c} V\ (\mathrm{V}) & 0 & 4 & 8 & 12 & 16 & 20 \\ \hline I\ (\mathrm{mA}) & 0 & 50 & 100 & 150 & 200 & 250 \end{array}$$

We replace the wire resistor with a $10\,\Omega$ resistor and successively increase the reading of the voltmeter by $2\,\mathrm{V}$ each time, up to and including $10\,\mathrm{V}$, recording in table (A2) the corresponding pairs of measured values.

TABLE A2

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c|c} V\ (\mathrm{V}) & 0 & 2 & 4 & 6 & 8 & 10 \\ \hline I\ (\mathrm{mA}) & 0 & 200 & 400 & 600 & 800 & 1000 \end{array}$$

We also replace the resistor with an incandescent lamp (200 V/10 W), repeating the previous procedure and filling in table (A3) with the values of the readings.

TABLE A3

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c|c} V\ (\mathrm{V}) & 0 & 4 & 8 & 12 & 16 & 20 \\ \hline I\ (\mathrm{mA}) & 0 & 10 & 18 & 24 & 28 & 30 \end{array}$$

D1.2 On a system of I–V axes, plot the pairs of readings for the heater wire and draw the corresponding graph as accurately as possible. Do the same for the resistor.

D1.3 What is the form of the graphs for the wire and the resistor? From the form of the graphs, calculate the values of their resistances. What is the more general finding, and by which law is this form covered?

D1.4 Also plot the I–V graph for the incandescent lamp. What is the form of its characteristic? Does this form obey the law you referred to previously?

D1.5 Calculate from the graph the resistance of the heating lamp for the voltage values $V_1 = 6\,\mathrm{V}$, $V_2 = 14\,\mathrm{V}$ and $V_3 = 20\,\mathrm{V}$. What conclusion follows about the relation between the resistance of the lamp and its temperature, which increases as the voltage increases?

D2. I–V CHARACTERISTIC OF A CRYSTAL DIODE

We set up a series circuit that includes a DC power supply (0–20 V), a switch, an ohmic resistor to limit the current and protect the diode, a p-n crystal diode, an ideal ammeter and an ideal voltmeter connected across the crystal diode.

D2.1 Draw the electric circuits with the crystal diode connected first in forward and then in reverse bias.

In the circuit containing the crystal diode connected in forward bias, we close the switch and increase the voltage supplied by the power supply, so that voltmeter readings across the crystal diode between 0 and 0.8 V are observed. These readings are recorded together with the corresponding ammeter readings in table B1.

TABLE B1

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c} V\ (\mathrm{V}) & 0 & 0.2 & 0.4 & 0.6 & 0.65 & 0.70 & 0.75 & 0.78 & 0.79 \\ \hline I\ (\mathrm{mA}) & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0.2 & 1.0 & 2.0 & 6.0 & 20.0 & 30.0 \end{array}$$

We open the switch and interchange the connecting leads of the power supply, so that the polarity of the source is reversed and thus the crystal diode is in reverse bias. We also reverse the polarities of the instruments and close the switch. The readings of the instruments are taken for values of the supply voltage in steps of 4 V from 0 to 20 V and are recorded in table B2.

TABLE B2

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c|c} V\ (\mathrm{V}) & 0 & -4 & -8 & -12 & -16 & -20 \\ \hline I\ (\mathrm{mA}) & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \end{array}$$

D2.2 Plot on V–I axes (with a different voltage scale) the pairs of instrument readings of table B1 (forward bias) and draw the graph, obtaining the characteristic curve $I = f(V)$ of the crystal diode.

D2.3 From the form of the diagrams and the values in the tables, what do you conclude about the way the current varies as a function of the voltage? What resistance does the crystal diode present in relation to the voltage and the way it is biased?

D2.4 Draw the 6 circuits with the elements given below and select those in which the lamp lights up.

• Circuit 1 with a source, a lamp and a p-n junction in forward bias
• Circuit 2 with a source, a lamp and 2 p-n junctions in forward bias in series
• Circuit 3 with a source, a lamp and a p-n junction in reverse bias
• Circuit 4 with a source, a lamp and 2 p-n junctions in parallel in forward bias
• Circuit 5 with a source, a lamp and 2 p-n junctions in series, one in forward bias and one in reverse bias
• Circuit 6 with a source, a lamp and 2 p-n junctions in parallel, one in forward bias and one in reverse bias

[2 + 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 + 2 + 3 + 3 + 3 marks]

problems.title: Problem A
problems.problem:
Problem A

A1. A body is released at time $t_o = 0$ to fall freely. If $\Delta h_{\nu-1}$ is the distance the body covers in the $(\nu-1)$-th second and $\Delta h_\nu$ is the distance it covers in the $\nu$-th second, then the difference $\Delta h_\nu - \Delta h_{\nu-1}$

(a) is constant and equal to $g$

(b) is constant and equal to $\dfrac{g}{2}$

(c) increases linearly with time

(d) increases exponentially with time

i. Which is the correct answer?

ii. Justify your choice.

[2 + 10 marks]

A2. On the glass surface of a horizontal table we move a volume of a dictionary with acceleration of magnitude $\dfrac{g}{3}$, by exerting a constant horizontal force of magnitude $F$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2022-3-1-fig1.png

Next we place the dictionary in contact with an identical, sturdy vertical glass pane and exert a horizontal force of the same magnitude F perpendicular to its surface, which passes through its centre of mass. The dictionary slides vertically downwards with acceleration of magnitude $\dfrac{7g}{12}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2022-3-1-fig2.png

The value of the coefficient of friction between the glass surface and the surface of the dictionary is:

(a) $\dfrac{1}{3}$ (b) $\dfrac{2}{3}$ (c) $\dfrac{1}{2}$ (d) $\dfrac{3}{4}$

i. Which is the correct answer?

ii. Justify your choice.

[2 + 13 marks]

problems.title: Problem B
problems.problem:
Problem B

B1. Every morning Anastasia has a constant worry about whether she will catch the bus that takes her to her school. Today, running with speed $\upsilon_\mathrm{A} = 4\,\mathrm{m/s}$, and while at time $t_o = 0$ she is at a distance $d = 15\,\mathrm{m}$ from the stop, she notices that the bus starts to move away with constant acceleration $\alpha = 0.5\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2022-3-2-fig1.jpg

B1.1. Without changing her pace, she manages to catch up with it at time $t_1$. Calculate the time $t_1$.

B1.2. Calculate the distance of the bus from the stop at time $t_1$.

B1.3. Calculate the magnitude of the velocity of the bus at time $t_1$.

B1.4. The equations also predict a second “meeting” of Anastasia and the bus, which would occur if at time $t_1$ she did not get on and she and the bus continued their motion in the same way. For this theoretical possibility, calculate the time $t_2$ at which the second meeting would occur.

B1.5. Calculate the distance Anastasia will have covered from time $t_o = 0$ to time $t_2$.

B1.6. Calculate the magnitude of the velocity of the bus at time $t_2$.

B1.7. Calculate the maximum distance of Anastasia from the bus, from time $t_1$ to time $t_2$.

B1.8. After her morning over-effort, Anastasia thought of solving, as a physics exercise, the case in which, running more slowly with a minimum speed of magnitude $\upsilon_\mathrm{min}$, she would just barely catch the bus. Calculate $\upsilon_\mathrm{min}$ as well.

B1.9. Running with a speed of magnitude $\upsilon_\mathrm{min}$ she would catch the bus at time $t_3$. Calculate the time $t_3$.

B1.10. Calculate the magnitude of the velocity of the bus at time $t_3$.

B1.11. Her parents, in any case, advised her, since it is dangerous to run after the bus, to set off from home a little earlier, so that with speed $\upsilon_\mathrm{A} = 4\,\mathrm{m/s}$ she reaches it at the stop exactly at the moment it is ready to leave. Calculate this time interval.

Assume that Anastasia and the school bus (the entrance door of the school bus) have small dimensions and move continuously along the same straight line.

[1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 marks]

B2. In a warehouse there is a horizontal platform of height H and length H. At the edge of the platform, and without touching it, there are $\nu$ cubic homogeneous boxes, each of mass m and edge d, placed one on top of the other, as shown in the figure (initial position of the boxes).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2022-3-2-fig2.png

(left) Initial position of the boxes; (right) Moving the boxes. Labels: ΓΕΡΑΝΟΣ = crane, ν ΚΙΒΩΤΙΑ = ν boxes, ΠΛΑΤΦΟΡΜΑ = platform.

For the lengths mentioned, $H = \nu d$ holds. A crane lifts the boxes one by one and places each on the platform so that it touches the edge of the platform. A worker pushes each box with a horizontal force and carries it to the other end of the platform, until it touches the previous one. The boxes have a coefficient of kinetic friction μ (which is equal to the coefficient of limiting static friction) with the platform. In the end all the boxes are on the platform, placed one next to the other, so that the last one touches the edge of the platform (final position of the boxes).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2022-3-2-fig3.png

Final position of the boxes

Given $\nu$, m, μ, d and the acceleration due to gravity g, calculate the minimum work of the forces required to move the boxes from the initial position to the final position.

The sum of the first $\nu$ terms of an arithmetic progression, $S_\nu = \dfrac{(\alpha_1+\alpha_\nu)\nu}{2}$, is given. Air resistance is considered negligible.

[10 marks]

problems.title: Problem C
problems.problem:
Problem C

Space travel has had (and continues to have) as its ultimate goal the scientific exploration of space. For this purpose (unfortunately also for military purposes) rockets were developed. From the first rocket, the R-7 ICBM, which was used for space research in the launch of Sputnik in 1957, until today, a great deal of progress has been made in the development of rocket technology.

A rocket of height $H = 40\,\mathrm{m}$ stands vertically on the ground at the launch site. Right at the tip of the rocket is the launch tower. At a distance $h = 15\,\mathrm{m}$ from the ground, on the outer side of the rocket, at position Α, there is a small insulating tile. At time $t_o = 0$ the rocket starts to lift off with a constant vertical acceleration of magnitude $\alpha = 2\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$. At the instant when the tile passes the height of the launch tower, it comes unstuck from the rocket and moves vertically under the action of its weight only.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2022-3-3-fig1.png

Labels: εξέδρα = launch tower, έδαφος = ground.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2022-3-3-fig2.jpg

Calculate:

C1. the times $t_1$, $t_2$ at which the tile passes the height of the tower.

C2. the time $t_{o\lambda}$ at which the tile reaches the ground and comes to rest, without bouncing.

C3. the maximum height above the ground that the tile will reach.

C4. the vertical distance of the tile from position Α of the rocket at time $t_3 = 8\,\mathrm{s}$.

C5. the vertical distance of the tile from position Α of the rocket at time $t_4 = 10\,\mathrm{s}$.

The magnitude of the acceleration due to gravity $g = 10\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$ is given. Air resistance is to be considered negligible.

[5 + 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 marks]

problems.title: Problem 1
problems.problem:
Problem 1

An ideal massless spring of constant k with natural length $L$ is vertical, with its upper end fixed at an immovable point. A small body (Σ) of mass m hangs from the lower end of the spring and is at rest, while the spring has an extension equal to $d$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2023-1-fig1.png

Next, we place the spring–body system in a smooth vertical quarter circle ΑΓ of radius $R=L$ and centre K, so that its axis is horizontal and coincides with the horizontal radius of the quarter circle. The small body (Σ) touches the upper end Α of the quarter circle, while remaining joined to one end of the spring. The other end of the spring is connected to the centre K of the quarter circle in such a way that the spring–body system can rotate without friction. We release the body (Σ) from the end Α, free to move. The body (Σ) passes through the lower end Γ of the quarter circle and continues to move on a smooth horizontal plane, without ever losing contact with it. The body (Σ) stops momentarily after travelling a distance x on the horizontal plane. The distance x is equal to

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2023-1-fig2.png

(a) $\sqrt{L\cdot(d+\sqrt{2\cdot L\cdot d})}$

(b) $\sqrt{2\cdot L\cdot(d+\sqrt{2\cdot L\cdot d})}$

(c) $\sqrt{L\cdot(2\cdot d+\sqrt{2\cdot L\cdot d})}$

(d) $\sqrt{2\cdot L\cdot(2\cdot d+\sqrt{2\cdot L\cdot d})}$

A. Choose the correct answer. [2 marks]

B. Justify your choice. [10 marks]

problems.title: Problem 2
problems.problem:
Problem 2

In the microcosm there are many small particles, which we call elementary particles. Apart from the well-known ones (proton, electron, neutron, photon), the rest live for a very short time interval. Consequently, they decay quickly (spontaneously) and form other particles. There are detectors, which we have built at research centres in order to study them, in which we can distinguish the trajectories of the charged particles inside a homogeneous magnetic field. The neutral particles we can distinguish indirectly, from the processing of the data of the charged particles.

Suppose that in a detector we see the decay:

$$\mathrm{K}^o\rightarrow\pi^{+}+e^{-}+\ldots$$

that is, the decay of the neutral kaon $\mathrm{K}^o$ into a positively charged pion $\pi^{+}$ and an electron $e^{-}$. The dots indicate that there may also be other particles which, if they are neutral, we do not see in the detector. The trajectories of the particles are perpendicular to the field lines of a homogeneous magnetic field of intensity $\vec{B}$ with direction from the page towards the reader, whose cross-section is a square ΑΓΔΕ of side $\dfrac{5\alpha}{4}$, where $\alpha$ is a constant length. The particle $\mathrm{K}^o$ was created at the point Z and decayed at the point Η (we do not see its trajectory because it is uncharged). The point Η is at a distance $\dfrac{\alpha}{4}$ from the two sides ΔΕ and ΕΑ. The straight segment ΖΗ is parallel to the side ΕΑ. The figure shows the two trajectories (1) and (2) of the two particles produced by the decay of the kaon. The velocity $\vec{\upsilon}_1$ of one particle has the direction ΖΗ, while the velocity $\vec{\upsilon}_2$ of the other particle makes an angle $\varphi=60^o$ with the velocity $\vec{\upsilon}_1$, as shown in the figure. The particle of trajectory (1) leaves from the vertex Γ with velocity perpendicular to the side ΓΔ.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2023-2-fig1.png

(a) Which trajectory corresponds to the pion and which to the electron? Justify your answer. [5 marks]

(b) Someone might claim that in this decay the principle of conservation of momentum is violated. On what experimental data is such a claim based? Give him a logical argument, based on the experiment we perform, which shows that the conservation of momentum is not violated. [5 marks]

(c) The particle of trajectory (2) leaves the magnetic field from a point Λ. Calculate the distance ΗΛ as a function of the length $\alpha$. [5 marks]

(d) If $t_\pi$ and $t_e$ are the times of motion of the pion and of the electron respectively in the magnetic field, find the ratio $\dfrac{t_\pi}{t_e}$. [5 marks]

We consider the weights of the particles negligible. The mass of the pion is 264 times greater than the mass of the electron. The magnitude of the velocity of the electron is 132 times greater than the magnitude of the velocity of the pion. The charge of the pion has the same magnitude as the charge of the electron $\left(q_e=-q_\pi=-e\right)$.

problems.title: Problem 3
problems.problem:
Problem 3

A point body of mass $\mathrm{m}=1\,\mathrm{kg}$ is connected to the end of an ideal spring of constant $\mathrm{k}=4\cdot\pi^2\,\mathrm{N/m}$. The system, under the action of a driver, performs a forced oscillation. The driver supplies energy to the system 4 times every 2 seconds. The ratio of the maximum kinetic energy $\mathrm{K_{max}}$ of the body to the maximum potential energy $\mathrm{U_{max}}$ of the oscillation is:

(a) $1$ (b) $2$ (c) $4$ (d) $\dfrac{1}{4}$

A. Choose the correct answer. [2 marks]

B. Justify your choice. [8 marks]

problems.title: Problem 4
problems.problem:
Problem 4

The homogeneous wheel of the adjacent figure has radius $R=2\,m$ and rolls without slipping. Let A be a point of the wheel which is at a distance $r=1\,m$ above the centre of mass of the wheel and on the same vertical line as it. The wheel starts at time $t=0$, with no initial velocity, accelerating with an acceleration of magnitude $a_{cm}=2\,m/s^2$. The magnitude of the acceleration of the point A at time $t=1\,s$ is:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2023-4-fig1.png

(a) $\sqrt{2}\,m/s^2$ (b) $\sqrt{3}\,m/s^2$ (c) $\sqrt{5}\,m/s^2$ (d) $\sqrt{10}\,m/s^2$

A. Choose the correct answer. [2 marks]

B. Justify your choice. [8 marks]

problems.title: Problem 5
problems.problem:
Problem 5

A homogeneous vertical rectangular door has a width $\ell$ four times its height $d$ and is supported by hinges at its two ends on a vertical wall. The direction of the force from the lower hinge passes through the midpoint of its upper side. The ratio of the magnitudes of the forces exerted by the upper and the lower hinge respectively is:

(a) $\sqrt{5}$ (b) $2\sqrt{5}$ (c) $\dfrac{\sqrt{5}}{5}$ (d) $\dfrac{2\sqrt{5}}{5}$

A. Choose the correct answer. [2 marks]

B. Justify your choice. [10 marks]

problems.title: Problem 6
problems.problem:
Problem 6

A homogeneous beam of length $\ell$ and weight w is in limiting equilibrium between two vertical walls, one of which is smooth, while with the other there is friction at their point of contact, with coefficient μ. The distance between the walls is equal to:

(a) $\dfrac{\ell}{\sqrt{\mu^2+4}}$ (b) $\dfrac{2\ell}{\sqrt{\mu^2+4}}$ (c) $\dfrac{\ell}{\sqrt{\mu^2-4}}$ (d) $\dfrac{2\ell}{\sqrt{\mu^2-4}}$

A. Choose the correct answer. [2 marks]

B. Justify your choice. [10 marks]

problems.title: Problem 7
problems.problem:
Problem 7

The magnitude of the magnetic field at the centre of a circular current-carrying conductor of radius r carrying a current $I_1=10\,mA$ is $B_1$. An electric charge $q=50\,\mathrm{\mu C}$ moves with frequency f on a circular path of radius r, at the centre of which the magnitude of the magnetic field is $B_2=2B_1$. The frequency of rotation of the electric charge is:

(a) $100\,\mathrm{Hz}$ (b) $200\,\mathrm{Hz}$ (c) $400\,\mathrm{Hz}$ (d) $1000\,\mathrm{Hz}$

A. Choose the correct answer. [2 marks]

B. Justify your choice. [10 marks]

problems.title: Problem 8
problems.problem:
Problem 8

On a glass, non-elastic table, the bodies $\Sigma_2$ and $\Sigma_3$, with masses $m_2$ and $m_3$ respectively, are in equilibrium, tied to an ideal spring of constant k. The breaking limit of the table is $T_\theta$. From a height h we release a sphere of mass $m_1$, which collides centrally, elastically and instantaneously with the body $\Sigma_2$. We do not want the table to break, but we also do not want the body $\Sigma_3$ to lose contact with the table. Given are the magnitude of the acceleration of gravity g, $m_1=m$, $m_2=3m$, $m_3=3m$ and $T_\theta=12mg$. The maximum height h for which both constraints are satisfied is:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2023-8-fig1.png

(a) $\dfrac{12mg}{k}$ (b) $\dfrac{24mg}{k}$ (c) $\dfrac{36mg}{k}$ (d) $\dfrac{48mg}{k}$

A. Choose the correct answer. [2 marks]

B. Justify your choice. [10 marks]

problems.title: Problem A
problems.problem:
Problem A

A1. Two identical, small, metal spheres, charged with unequal positive charges $Q_1$ and $Q_2$ for which $Q_1>Q_2$, interact with forces of magnitude $F_1$. The spheres are brought into contact with insulating tongs for a sufficient time and then moved apart to the same distance as initially, so that the magnitude of the interaction force becomes $F_2$. For the magnitudes of the interaction forces:

(a) $F_2<F_1$ (b) $F_2>F_1$

(c) $F_2=F_1$ (d) we cannot answer

A. Which is the correct answer? [2 marks]

B. Justify your choice. [6 marks]

A2. A solid disc of radius R rotates in a horizontal plane about a vertical axis through its centre, with constant angular velocity of magnitude ω. From position A, which is at height $h=10R$ above point K of the circumference of the disc and on the same vertical line, a small ball is thrown horizontally with speed of magnitude $\upsilon_o$, so as to fall into a hole located at point Λ, diametrically opposite to point K on the circumference of the disc, and after the disc has performed 5 revolutions during the time of its motion. The magnitude of the acceleration of gravity is equal to g. The value of the angular velocity of rotation of the disc is equal to:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2023-2-1-fig1.png

(a) $\dfrac{5\pi g}{\upsilon_o}$ (b) $\dfrac{2\pi g}{\upsilon_o}$ (c) $\dfrac{\pi g}{\upsilon_o}$ (d) $\dfrac{\pi g}{2\upsilon_o}$

A. Which is the correct answer? [2 marks]

B. Justify your choice. [6 marks]

A3. A body is released from point A. After moving along the vertical quarter-circle AK, it then moves on a horizontal plane and finally goes up an inclined plane until it stops at point B. Throughout its motion the body has a coefficient of kinetic friction μ with the surfaces on which it moves. If T is the value of the friction at the various points of the path, then

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2023-2-1-fig2.png

(a) $T_\Lambda>T_K>T_M$ (b) $T_K\ge T_\Lambda>T_M$ (c) $T_K=T_\Lambda>T_M$

(d) $T_K>T_\Lambda\ge T_M$ (e) $T_\Lambda>T_K>T_M$ (f) $T_K>T_\Lambda>T_M$

A. Which is the correct answer? [2 marks]

B. Justify your choice. [7 marks]

problems.title: Problem B
problems.problem:
Problem B

B1. A small body is thrown with a horizontal velocity of magnitude $\upsilon_o$ at the instant $t_o=0$ from a point A, which is at a height h above the horizontal ground. The imaginary vertical line through point A meets the ground at a point O. We consider that only its weight, which is a constant force, acts on the body. On reaching the ground, the body has a velocity which makes a large angle with the ground. Let g be the magnitude of the acceleration of gravity. The distance of the body from point O is maximum at the instant:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2023-2-2-fig1.png

(a) $t=\dfrac{\sqrt{hg-\upsilon_o^2}}{2g}$ (b) $t=\dfrac{\sqrt{2\left(hg-\upsilon_o^2\right)}}{2g}$

(c) $t=\dfrac{\sqrt{hg-\upsilon_o^2}}{g}$ (d) $t=\dfrac{\sqrt{2\left(hg-\upsilon_o^2\right)}}{g}$

A. Which is the correct answer? [2 marks]

B. Justify your choice. [11 marks]

B2. A metal sphere is on a smooth horizontal plane and moves with velocity of constant magnitude υ. At the instant $t_o=0$ it is at position A, at a distance d from a point O, and its velocity makes an angle $\theta=30^o$ with the straight line segment AO, as shown in the figure. At point O there is an electromagnet which, at the appropriate instant, is switched on, so that it exerts an attractive force on the sphere, which then performs uniform circular motion with centre the point O. At some other instant the electromagnet is switched off and the sphere, without having completed a full circular orbit, passes again through point A at the instant $t_1$. The instant $t_1$ is equal to:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2023-2-2-fig2.png

(a) $\dfrac{d(\sqrt{3}+2\pi)}{3\upsilon}$ (b) $\dfrac{d(2\sqrt{3}+2\pi)}{3\upsilon}$

(c) $\dfrac{d(3\sqrt{3}+2\pi)}{3\upsilon}$ (d) $\dfrac{d(3+2\pi)}{3\upsilon}$

A. Which is the correct answer? [2 marks]

B. Justify your choice. [10 marks]

problems.title: Problem C
problems.problem:
Problem C

C1. The wheel of an amusement park (Ferris wheel) of radius R has 8 baskets of small dimensions (compared with the size of the wheel) and rotates clockwise with period T and constant angular velocity of magnitude ω. At the instant $t_o=0$, when basket (1) is at the highest point of its path, a small piece of it comes loose and falls at the instant $t_1$ into basket (3), without striking any other object during its motion, during which the piece can pass between the metal support of basket 2 without striking it. Baskets (1) and (3) are a quarter-circle apart along their circular path. From the instant $t_o=0$ to the instant $t_1$ the wheel has turned through a central angle φ. Take air resistance to be negligible. The acceleration of gravity g has a constant value. The radius R is given by the relation:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2023-2-3-fig1.png

(a) $R=\dfrac{g\mathrm{T}^2(1+\sin\varphi)}{8\pi^2}$ (b) $R=\dfrac{g\mathrm{T}^2(1-\sin\varphi)}{8\pi^2}$

(c) $R=\dfrac{g\mathrm{T}^2(1+\cos\varphi)}{8\pi^2}$ (d) $R=\dfrac{g\mathrm{T}^2(1-\cos\varphi)}{8\pi^2}$

A. Which is the correct answer? [2 marks]

B. Justify your choice. [10 marks]

C2. The uniform circular conductor AMKP, of uniform cross-section, has total resistance R, radius r and a small gap between the points A and P. The radius OK is fixed and immovable, while OA is conductively hinged at O and has at A a circular metal guide (ring), so that it can rotate without friction on the semicircle AMK, remaining in contact with it at all times. The radii OK and OA are conducting and have negligible ohmic resistance. The source has emf E and negligible internal resistance. We start rotating the radius OA clockwise (as the hands of a clock rotate). The current I through the arrangement as a function of the central angle φ swept by the radius OA, for the rotation from the initial position OA until just before it reaches the position OK for the first time, is given by the relation:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2023-2-3-fig2.png

(a) $I=\dfrac{2E\varphi}{\pi R}$ (b) $I=\dfrac{2\pi E}{R\left(\pi-\varphi\right)}$ (c) $I=\dfrac{\pi E}{R(\pi-\varphi)}$ (d) $I=\dfrac{2\pi E}{3R\varphi}$

A. Which is the correct answer? [2 marks]

B. Justify your choice. [11 marks]

problems.title: Problem D (Experimental part)
problems.problem:
Problem D (Experimental part)

In a potato we insert a galvanised screw and a 0.5 euro coin. Using wires with crocodile clips, we connect in turn resistors of the values shown in the table below. Using an ideal voltmeter we measure each time the voltage across the resistor, and using an ideal ammeter we measure the current through the resistor each time.

D1. Draw the circuit described above, placing the measuring instruments correctly.

D2. The values we measured are shown in the table. Using the table, plot the V–I graph and determine the characteristics of the potato battery, i.e. its emf and its internal resistance.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c} \text{Ohmic resistance of conductor} & \text{Voltage across the battery} & \text{Current in the circuit} & \text{Power delivered by the battery to the circuit} \\ \text{in } \mathrm{k\Omega} & \text{in } \mathrm{V} & \text{in } \mathrm{\mu A} & \text{in } \mathrm{\mu W} \\ \hline \text{none} & 0.94 & 0 & \\ 20 & 0.74 & 37 & \\ 10 & 0.61 & 60 & \\ 5 & 0.46 & 90 & \\ 2 & 0.28 & 133 & \\ 1 & 0.17 & 155 & \\ 0.5 & 0.1 & 168 & \end{array}$$

D3. Copy the last column of the table, completed, into your answer script and plot the graph of the power as a function of the current.

D4. From the graph, find the maximum power that the battery can deliver to the circuit. Find the value of the resistance of the resistor that you must place in the circuit in order to have the maximum power.

D5. Prove theoretically that the maximum power delivered to the circuit occurs when the resistance of the resistor we connect is equal to the internal resistance of our battery.

D6. If we had only 4 resistors, what values should their resistances have had, and what should we have done to carry out exactly the same experiment, so that exactly the same measurements would be obtained?

[4 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 5 marks]

problems.title: Problem 1
problems.problem:
Problem 1

As the skier, of mass $70\,\mathrm{kg}$, goes down the plane slope of inclination angle φ, he experiences the force of air resistance, whose magnitude is of the form $F_\alpha=k\cdot\upsilon^2$, where k is a constant that depends on the density of the air and on the area of the skier's surface and has the value $k=0.36\,\mathrm{kg/m}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2023-3-1-fig1.jpg

The coefficient of kinetic friction between the skier's skis and the slope is $\mu=0.4$, and the magnitude of the acceleration of gravity is given as $g=10\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$. For the angle φ, $\sin\varphi=0.6$ and $\cos\varphi=0.8$.

A. Describe in detail the type of motion performed by the skier as he goes down the slope.

B. The maximum speed that the skier will reach going down the slope is approximately equal to:

(i) $18.2\,\mathrm{m/s}$ (ii) $23.3\,\mathrm{m/s}$ (iii) $34.1\,\mathrm{m/s}$ (iv) $28.6\,\mathrm{m/s}$

[10 marks (5 + 5)]

problems.title: Problem 2
problems.problem:
Problem 2

A small car A is stopped at a traffic light. At the instant $t_o=0$ the light turns green and car A starts moving with constant acceleration of magnitude α, while at the same instant a second small car B, which moves continuously with constant velocity, passes beside it. At some instant car A starts decelerating with constant acceleration of the same magnitude α. At the instant when car A comes to rest, car B passes beside it. We denote by $d_1$ the maximum distance by which car A was ahead of car B and by $d_2$ the maximum distance by which car B was ahead of car A. We consider that the two cars move in parallel traffic lanes. The dimensions of the cars are considered negligible compared with the distances $d_1$ and $d_2$. The relation connecting the distances $d_1$ and $d_2$ is:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2023-3-2-fig1.jpg

(i) $d_2=d_1$ (ii) $d_2=2d_1$ (iii) $d_2=3d_1$ (iv) $d_2=4d_1$

[15 marks]

problems.title: Problem 3
problems.problem:
Problem 3

A helicopter hovers at a height of $18\,\mathrm{m}$ above the surface of the sea. A rescuer of the fire brigade's special forces, of mass $80\,\mathrm{kg}$, as part of his training, descends vertically with the help of a massless and inextensible rope which has a breaking limit $T=780\,\mathrm{N}$. The magnitude of the acceleration of gravity is given as $g=10\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$. Consider the dimensions of the man small and the effect of the air on the motion of the rescuer negligible. The rescuer is lowered tied to a rope, without making any effort himself.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2023-3-3-fig1.jpg

A. What would you advise them in order to lower him safely: to lower him with constant velocity or with constant acceleration, and why?

B. What is his smallest possible speed at the moment he reaches the surface of the sea, so that the rope does not break?

(i) $2\,\mathrm{m/s}$ (ii) $3\,\mathrm{m/s}$ (iii) $4\,\mathrm{m/s}$ (iv) $5\,\mathrm{m/s}$

[15 marks (5 + 10)]

problems.title: Problem 4
problems.problem:
Problem 4

A seagull on the beach, next to a vertical rock, finds a small shell. It snatches it and at the instant $t_o=0$ starts flying vertically upwards with constant acceleration of magnitude $\alpha=0.5\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$. At the instant $t_1=8\,\mathrm{s}$ it lets the shell fall. Three friends A, B, Γ are lying on the beach behind a bush and can see the rock from a height $\mathrm{H}=16\,\mathrm{m}$ upwards.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2023-3-4-fig1.png

A. A said that he did not see the shell at all, B said that he saw the shell travel a distance of $80\,\mathrm{cm}$ and Γ that he saw the shell travel a distance of $1.6\,\mathrm{m}$. Which of the three friends is right? Justify your answer.

B. At the instant $t_1=8\,\mathrm{s}$ a small pebble comes loose from the top of the rock and falls vertically. Let $\upsilon_\Pi$ and $\upsilon_\mathrm{K}$ be the magnitudes of the velocities that the pebble and the shell respectively have at each instant. Draw in your notebook, with full justification, the graph of the difference $\Delta\upsilon=\upsilon_\Pi-\upsilon_\mathrm{K}$ against the time t, from the instant $t_1=8\,\mathrm{s}$ to the instant $t_2=9\,\mathrm{s}$.

Air resistance is negligible and the magnitude of the acceleration of gravity is equal to $g=10\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$.

[15 marks (5 + 10)]

problems.title: Problem 5
problems.problem:
Problem 5

A thin board of weight w is held vertical at some height above the ground, as it is held between the palms of our hands. If we reduce the pressure between the board and our palms, the board, sliding, acquires an acceleration of magnitude $\alpha=0.1g$, while it receives a normal force $F=\dfrac{3w}{2}$ from each palm.

The coefficient of friction μ between each palm and the surface of the board is equal to:

(i) 0.3 (ii) 0.4 (iii) 0.5 (iv) 0.6

[10 marks]

problems.title: Problem 6
problems.problem:
Problem 6

Two bodies A and B move on parallel tracks and their distance, along the direction of their motion, is $d=198\,\mathrm{m}$, as also shown in the figure. At the instant $t_o=0\,\mathrm{s}$ a body Γ, which moves to the right with constant velocity $\upsilon_o=4\,\mathrm{m/s}$ on a track parallel to the others, is at the position $x_o=0\,\mathrm{m}$. At the same time, body B starts moving to the left with constant acceleration. Body A starts moving to the right after a time interval $\Delta t=3\,\mathrm{s}$ with constant acceleration of magnitude $\alpha_A=2\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$.

A. Write the equations of motion for the three bodies.

B. Calculate the instant and the position at which bodies A and Γ meet.

C. Calculate the magnitude of the acceleration of body B so that it reaches the same position x where A and Γ meet, at the same time as them.

D. Draw, on the same diagram in your notebook, the velocity–time graphs for the three bodies.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2023-3-6-fig1.png

[15 marks (3 + 3 + 3 + 6)]

problems.title: Problem 7 (Experimental part)
problems.problem:
Problem 7 (Experimental part)

In order to study the fall of a body we use the arrangement in the photograph.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2023-3-7-fig1.jpg

The arrangement consists of an electromagnet at the top, which holds an iron ball. Below the electromagnet there are two photogates. By pressing the appropriate button of the timer, the current through the electromagnet is interrupted while at the same time the measurement of time begins. Falling, the ball passes first through the upper photogate and then through the lower one. Thus the instrument finally gives us two times $t_1$ and $t_2$. The time $t_1$ is the time from the instant the current was interrupted, so that the ball was released, until the instant it passed through the first photogate. The time $t_2$ is the time from the instant the current was interrupted and the ball was released until the instant it passed through the second photogate.

Each time we can change the position of the photogates and measure the distance between the two photogates. The measurements we took were the following:

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c} \Delta h & t_1 & t_2 & t_2^2-t_1^2 \\ (\mathrm{cm}) & (\mathrm{ms}) & (\mathrm{ms}) & (\mathrm{s^2}) \\ \hline 10.5 & 122.4 & 193.2 & \\ 15.5 & 122.3 & 218.2 & \\ 20.8 & 123 & 243.2 & \\ 28.5 & 122.5 & 274.1 & \\ 36.4 & 123.2 & 303.3 & \end{array}$$

From these measurements we want to check two things:

1. Whether the motion is rectilinear and uniformly accelerated.

2. In case it is rectilinear and uniformly accelerated, how large the acceleration of the motion is.

To answer the first question we plot the graph $\Delta h=f(t_2^2-t_1^2)$.

1. Complete the 4th column of the table, writing the values with the correct number of decimal digits, and plot the above graph on graph paper. What does its slope represent?

2. Find for each measurement the acceleration, and the mean value of the acceleration of the motion, with the correct number of decimal digits.

3. Find the largest value of the acceleration as well as the smallest one. Determine the spread of the acceleration $\Delta a=a_{max}-a_{min}$.

4. Considering that the error of the measurement is equal to half the spread, $\delta\alpha=\Delta\alpha/2$, write the acceleration in the form $a=\bar{a}\pm\delta a$.

5. What conclusions do you draw about the two hypotheses above that you wanted to check?

6. If you know that the acceleration of gravity in the laboratory where the experiment was performed is $g=981\,\mathrm{cm/s^2}$, what interpretation do you give to your conclusions?

[20 marks (4 + 3 + 4 + 3 + 3 + 3)]

problems.title: Problem 1
problems.problem:
Problem 1

When a small elastic ball is released from some height above a smooth horizontal floor and falls freely, we expect it to rise back to its initial height after the elastic collision. With the following technique a small ball can behave like a “super ball”, bouncing back after the collision to a considerably greater height: from a point at height h, two small elastic balls with masses $m_1=3m$ and $m_2=m$ are released to fall simultaneously. The first collides head-on and elastically with the floor and, at the moment it leaves the floor, it collides again head-on and elastically with the second ball, which is coming down. After the collision, the ball of mass $m_2$ will shoot up to a height H equal to:

Problem 2

The spring (ideal) – mass system, with spring constant $k$ and a mass $M$, performs simple harmonic oscillation, as in the picture, above a motion sensor. The sensor measures the velocity of the mass $M$. In Experiment 1, $M=M_1=1.0\,\mathrm{kg}$ and $k=k_1$. In Experiment 2, $M=M_2=4.0\,\mathrm{kg}$ and $k=k_2$. The results of the two (2) experiments for one (1) period of the simple harmonic oscillations are given in the graph below:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2024-2-fig2.png

The ratio $\dfrac{k_1}{k_2}$ is equal to:

problems.title: Problem 3
problems.problem:
Problem 3

A homogeneous cylinder is wound with a thin, massless and inextensible string and is in equilibrium on the inclined plane, as shown in the figure. If the string AB is vertical and the angle of the inclined plane with the vertical direction is $\varphi$, then the ratio $\lambda$ of the tension of the string to the weight of the cylinder is given by the relation:

problems.title: Problem 4
problems.problem:
Problem 4

The body Σ performs a vertical simple harmonic oscillation due to the rotational motion of the wheel T, which is converted into a reciprocating motion through the connection of the system with the rigid rod AB (that is, as the wheel T rotates, the body Σ moves up and down). The points A and B are freely rotating joints with negligible friction. On top of the body Σ we have placed a body of mass m. https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2024-4-fig1.png

problems.title: Problem 5
problems.problem:
Problem 5

The foundation of a building comprises a rectangular homogeneous slab made of concrete and steel reinforcement, embedded in the ground. The building comprises a self-contained structure which rests on the foundation not rigidly but with the possibility of sliding, with a coefficient of limiting (static) friction between them equal to $\mu=0.2$. A seismic event with period $T=1\,\mathrm{s}$ sets the system of the foundation together with the building into oscillation. The maximum amplitude of the oscillation for which the building does not slide on its base is equal to:

(A) $4\,\mathrm{cm}$ (B) $5\,\mathrm{cm}$ (C) $8\,\mathrm{cm}$ (D) $10\,\mathrm{cm}$

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2024-5-fig1.png

problems.title: Problem 6

Problem 6

A body of mass m moves with momentum of magnitude P and collides centrally and elastically with a stationary body of mass M. After the collision the initially stationary body acquires the maximum possible momentum. For the magnitude of the momentum acquired by the body of mass M and the relation between the masses it holds that:

(A) $P_M=1.25P$ and $M<m$

(B) $P_M=1.5P$ and $M>m$

problems.title: Problem 7
problems.problem:
Problem 7

On a smooth horizontal square table ΑΒΓΔ of side $\alpha=4\,\mathrm{m}$, standing at a great height, there are three small spheres $\Sigma_1$, $\Sigma_2$ and $\Sigma_3$ at rest, with masses m, 3m and 3m respectively. The sphere $\Sigma_1$ is tied to one end of a massless and inextensible string of length $\ell=\dfrac{\alpha}{2}=2\,\mathrm{m}$, the other end of which is tied immovably at the centre O of the table. The string can rotate without friction about the point O. The string is always taut. The sphere $\Sigma_2$ is at a point E of the side ΓΔ, while the sphere $\Sigma_3$ is at a point Z of the side ΑΓ. The straight segment OE is parallel to the side ΑΓ, while the straight segment OZ is parallel to the side ΓΔ. The string makes an angle $\theta=45^\circ$ with the straight segment OE. At time $t_0=0$ we give the body $\Sigma_1$ a velocity of magnitude $\upsilon=10\,\dfrac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{s}}$, with direction perpendicular to the string and sense towards the side ΓΔ, as shown in the figure. Calculate the distance between the spheres $\Sigma_2$ and $\Sigma_3$ at the moment when the body $\Sigma_3$ leaves the table.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2024-7-fig1.png

Top view

It is given that air resistance is negligible, $\pi=3.1$ and the magnitude of the acceleration of gravity is $g=10\,\dfrac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{s^2}}$. All collisions of the bodies are to be considered central and elastic.

problems.title: Problem 1
problems.problem:
Problem 1

The diameter of electrical wires is specified by the gauge scale, by an integer that corresponds to a defined value in mm. As a wire becomes thinner, with a smaller diameter, the gauge value increases. A 12-gauge diameter corresponds to $2.053\,\mathrm{mm}$, a 14-gauge diameter corresponds to $1.628\,\mathrm{mm}$, while 10-gauge corresponds to $2.588\,\mathrm{mm}$. A 12-gauge copper wire safely carries a current of $20\,\mathrm{A}$.

(a) At what rate is a $1\,\mathrm{m}$ length of this wire heated?

(b) What would similarly happen for a 12-gauge aluminium wire?

(c) Which type of aluminium wire would be safe (would produce the same thermal power)?

Given: $\rho_{Cu}=0.0179\,\mathrm{\mu\Omega\,m}$, $\rho_{Al}=0.0290\,\mathrm{\mu\Omega\,m}$.

problems.title: Problem 2
problems.problem:
Problem 2

The fuse $f_1$ contains a wire of resistance $R_1$ which melts if it is put under a voltage of $5\,\mathrm{V}$ and carries a current of $0.1\,\mathrm{A}$. A second fuse $f_2$ with resistance $R_2$ melts for the corresponding values $6\,\mathrm{V}$ and $0.2\,\mathrm{A}$.

(a) $f_1$ and $f_2$ are connected in series and the circuit is supplied by a voltage that increases progressively. For what value of the voltage will one of the fuses melt?

(b) $f_1$ and $f_2$ are connected in parallel to a source of variable voltage. For what value of the current through the source will one of the fuses melt?

problems.title: Problem 3
problems.problem:
Problem 3

Small aircraft have electrical systems with a voltage of $24\,\mathrm{V}$, while cars, with roughly the same electrical power requirements, have a voltage of $12\,\mathrm{V}$. It is claimed that this is because aircraft need thinner wires, which weigh less. Check this claim.

Assume that the wires in the two cases have approximately the same length.

problems.title: Problem 4
problems.problem:
Problem 4

A small object of mass m is tied to the free end of a vertical, massless and inextensible string hanging from a fixed point of the ceiling. At some instant the object is launched horizontally with initial kinetic energy equal to $K_0$, so that the string is deflected from the vertical and the body comes momentarily to rest at the position where the direction of the string makes an angle θ with the vertical direction and the tension of the string has a magnitude equal to half the magnitude of its weight. As the body returns towards its initial position, at the instant, say $t_1$, at which the direction of the string makes an angle φ with the vertical direction, the magnitudes of the tangential and the centripetal acceleration have the ratio $\dfrac{\alpha_\varepsilon}{\alpha_\kappa}=\dfrac{1}{2}$. Find:

(a) The values of the angles θ and φ.

(b) The percentage of the initial kinetic energy $K_0$ that has been converted into potential energy at the instant $t_1$.

(c) The magnitude and the direction of the rate of change of momentum at the instant $t_1$.

Air resistance and friction at the points where the string is attached are considered negligible.

Given: the acceleration of gravity equal to g;

$\sin 30^\circ=\cos 60^\circ=\dfrac{1}{2}$, $\cos 30^\circ=\sin 60^\circ=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$.

problems.title: Problem 5
problems.problem:
Problem 5

In the "Zartman" experiment, an apparatus is used to measure the speed of the molecules of a gas.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2024-2-5-fig1.png

A cylinder of radius $r=0.5\,\mathrm{m}$ rotates with constant angular velocity $\omega=60\pi\,\mathrm{rad/s}$ and, in a cross-section perpendicular to its axis, of circular shape, it has an entrance through which we can direct a beam of molecules of a gas. The inner surface of the cylinder has a special coating with a film on which a molecule leaves its mark if it strikes it. If the cylinder were at rest, a molecule after its entrance would travel the length of one diameter and would leave its mark on the opposite side, e.g. at a point A. When, however, the cylinder rotates, the mark of the molecule will be recorded at a point B that corresponds to an arc $\widehat{s}=\overset{\frown}{AB}$ with corresponding central angle $\theta=30^\circ$. In this way the speed u of the molecule is calculated to have magnitude:

(A) $200\,\mathrm{m/s}$ (B) $240\,\mathrm{m/s}$ (C) $300\,\mathrm{m/s}$ (D) $360\,\mathrm{m/s}$

Justify your answer.

problems.title: Problem 6
problems.problem:
Problem 6

A body moves on a circular path of radius $2.25\,\mathrm{m}$. At some instant $t_1$ the body has a linear velocity of magnitude $4.5\,\mathrm{m/s}$, increasing at a rate of $9\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2024-2-6-fig1.png

At that instant, the angle between the linear velocity and the acceleration of the body is:

(A) $90^\circ$ (B) $0^\circ$ (C) $45^\circ$ (D) $60^\circ$

Justify your answer.

problems.title: Problem 7
problems.problem:
Problem 7

A spacecraft of mass $m=10^{3}\,\mathrm{kg}$ is launched from the surface of the Earth with initial speed $u_0=\sqrt{\dfrac{18}{21}g_0R_\Gamma}$ and at an angle φ to the horizontal direction, with $0<\varphi<90^{o}$. The spacecraft, moving on an elliptical orbit, reaches a maximum height above the surface of the Earth $H=\dfrac{R_\Gamma}{2}$. Consider the Earth to be at rest. Given: $g_0=10\,\mathrm{\dfrac{m}{s^2}}$, $R_\Gamma=6400\,\mathrm{km}$ and $\pi=3.14$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2024-2-7-fig1.png

A.

(a) Prove that the spacecraft does not escape from the Earth's attraction.

(b) The momentum that must be given to the spacecraft, when it reaches the maximum height $H=\dfrac{R_\Gamma}{2}$, in order to put it into a circular orbit around the Earth of radius $r_1=R_\Gamma+H$.

(c) The work of the engine carried by the spacecraft in order to put it into the circular orbit of radius $r_1$.

(d) The period of revolution of the spacecraft on the circular orbit of radius $r_1$.

Neglect any forces that resist the motion of the spacecraft.

B. After some time on the circular orbit of radius $r_1$, at the instant $t_1$, the spacecraft enters a region with non-zero density of interplanetary gas, as a result of which it loses mechanical energy at an average rate $\lambda=1.2\cdot10^{5}\,\dfrac{\mathrm{J}}{\text{revolution}}$. The orbit of the spacecraft is a spiral, but to simplify the problem we shall assume that it is circular, with a "slowly decreasing radius".

(a) Calculate the distance $H_2$ of the spacecraft from the surface of the Earth and its period $T_2$ at the end of the 100th revolution after the instant $t_1$.

(b) Calculate the magnitude of the average retarding force during the 100 revolutions.

(c) Find the relation between the kinetic and the potential energy of the spacecraft at every point of its motion, and comment on the spiral orbit in terms of energy.

problems.title: Problem 1
problems.problem: A homogeneous rectangular door of mass m has width $3\ell$, height $\ell$ and is supported by two hinges, M1 at the upper end and M2 at the lower end, on a vertical wall. The force from hinge M1 is horizontal. If the hinges are placed at distances $\ell/4$ from the ends of the door and the force from M1 is again horizontal, find the change in the magnitude of the force from hinge M2.

problems.title: Problem 2
problems.problem:
A horizontal homogeneous beam has mass $m$, length $L$ and is in equilibrium on two vertical supports, $Y1$ and $Y2$, each of which is at a distance $L/4$ from the ends. At the middle of the beam an object of mass 3m is placed and is at rest. An internal explosion splits the object into two fragments $\Sigma1$ and $\Sigma2$ with masses $m_1, m_2$ respectively, and $m_2=2m_1$. The bodies $\Sigma1$ and $\Sigma2$ move without friction on the surface of the beam and head towards the supports $Y1$ and $Y2$ respectively.

(A) Find the relation between the forces $N_1, N_2$ exerted by the supports on $\Sigma1$ and $\Sigma2$ during their motion on the beam.

(B) Investigate whether the beam can overturn and show when this happens.

problems.title: Problem 3
problems.problem:
Two small identical bodies, of mass m=1kg each, are fixed to the end of two identical ideal springs which have spring constant k=100 N/m and natural length $\ell_o=1m$. The free ends of the springs are fixed at the same fixed point O so that the springs have their natural length and their axes lie on the same horizontal straight line, which passes through the centres of mass of the bodies and through the point O, as shown in the figure. At some instant we release the two bodies, which then move in the same vertical plane. The two bodies arrive simultaneously at the lowest point of their curved trajectory, with horizontal velocities of magnitudes $u_1, u_2$, whereupon they collide head-on and inelastically (they stick together).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2025-3-fig1.png

1) Find the magnitude of the velocity of each body just before the collision, as well as the extension of each spring at that moment.

2) Show that the combined body, immediately after the collision, performs SHM (simple harmonic motion) and find its period.

3) Find the amplitude of the oscillation of the combined body and write the displacement–time equation, taking the downward direction as positive.

4) At the instant $t_1=\frac{T}{12}$ from the start of time (t=0), calculate the rates $\frac{\Delta k}{\Delta t}_{(t_1)}$ and $\frac{\Delta p}{\Delta t}_{(t_1)}$. Also calculate the work of the resultant force $W_{\Sigma F}$ from the instant $\mathrm{t}=0$ to $t=t_1$.

5) Plot, on the same diagram, the graphs of the kinetic, the potential and the total energy of the oscillation as functions of time, with graduated axes, for the time interval $0\le t\le\frac{\pi}{2}\ s$.

Given: $g=10\,\frac{m}{s^2}$, $\sqrt{3}\cong 1{,}7$, $\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right)=0{,}5$, $\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right)=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$, $\sqrt{18{,}75}\cong 4{,}33$. Resistances are considered negligible.

problems.title: Problem 4
problems.problem:
In the figure alongside, the square frame of side $\alpha=0{,}4\,m$ was made from a wire of length $\ell_{\sigma\upsilon\rho}=40\,m$ which has resistance per unit length $R^*=0{,}05\,\Omega/m$. The frame is in a magnetic field $B_1$, perpendicular to the field lines, with the magnitude of the magnetic field varying with time according to the relation $B_1=2{,}5t$ (S.I). The electrical source has emf $E=8\,V$ and internal resistance r. A resistor has ohmic resistance $R_1=12\,\Omega$. A horizontally placed rod of length (ΚΛ)=1m and resistance $R_2=4\,\Omega$ is constantly in contact with the vertical wires (of negligible resistance). The rod is in a uniform magnetic field with $B_2=2\,T$, perpendicular to the field lines. Initially all the switches are open. At the instant t=0 we close the switch $\delta_1$ and observe that the rod is in equilibrium. The magnitude of the acceleration of gravity is given, g=10 m/s$^2$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2025-4-fig1.png

[Label in the figure: μονωτικό δάπεδο = insulating floor.]

A) Calculate the direction of B$_1$, the direction of B$_2$ and the mass of the rod, if you know that the conventional direction of the current flowing in the frame is anticlockwise (opposite to the direction of rotation of the hands of a clock) and in the rod it is directed from Κ to Λ. At some instant we open the switch δ$_1$ and at the same time close the switch δ$_2$. We observe that the rod continues to be in equilibrium.

B) Find the internal resistance of the source.

At some later instant we open the switch δ$_2$ and the rod starts to descend, remaining all the time inside the magnetic field of magnitude B$_2$.

C) Calculate the maximum electric power in the resistor R$_1$.

While the rod has acquired its terminal velocity, we close the switch δ$_3$.

D) Calculate the magnitude of the rate of change of the electric current in the coil at the instant we close the switch δ$_3$. Given $\mu_o=4\pi10^{-7}\,Tm/A$, $R_3=12\,\Omega$ and, for the ideal coil: length $\ell_\pi=20\pi\,cm$, cross-sectional area of one turn $A_\pi=0{,}1\,m^2$ and N$_\pi$=10$^3$ turns.

E) Calculate the maximum value of the energy of the magnetic field of the coil.

problems.title: Problem 1
problems.problem:
The children's toy "little aeroplane" consists of a small battery-powered aeroplane tied to one end of a massless, inextensible string of length $\ell = 1.75\,\mathrm{m}$. The other end of the string is hung from a fixed point of the ceiling, which is at a distance $h = 2.74\,\mathrm{m}$ from the floor. We deflect the little aeroplane from the vertical and, with its motor running, it begins to describe circular orbits in a horizontal plane with a frequency of 25 revolutions per minute.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2025-2-1-fig1.png

(A) Can a child of height $H = 1.49\,\mathrm{m}$ move around the room standing upright without the risk of being hit by the little aeroplane?

(B) What must the "safety" period of the motion be for there to be no risk?

(C) While the little aeroplane is rotating in the "safety" orbit, the string breaks and at the same time its motor stops working. At what point on the floor will the little aeroplane land, relative to the foot of the vertical through the centre of its orbit?

Given $g = 10\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$ and $\pi^2 = 10$.

problems.title: Problem 2
problems.problem:
In the figure alongside, the inclined plane with angle of inclination $\theta$ rotates with constant angular velocity $\omega$ $\left(\mathrm{\frac{rad}{s}}\right)$. If the body Σ is in equilibrium when it is at a distance $r\ (\mathrm{m})$ from the axis of rotation, calculate the minimum coefficient of friction so that the equilibrium is not disturbed. Given $g = 10\,\mathrm{\frac{m}{s^2}}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2025-2-2-fig1.png

problems.title: Problem 3
problems.problem:
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2025-2-3-fig1.png

[Heading in the figure: ΠΡΟΣΟΨΗ ΗΜΙΣΦΑΙΡΙΚΟΥ ΛΟΦΟΥ = front view of the hemispherical hill; ΣΧΗΜΑ 1 = Figure 1.]

A Grade 11 (Β΄ Λυκείου) student, one spring day, found himself at the highest point of a hemispherical hill (see Figure 1). The hemispherical hill has been shaped so that from the left half of the hemisphere there is easy and safe access to its top for visitors. The right half of the hemisphere is smooth. A team of technicians has installed sensitive sensors, which detect contact over the whole right half of the hemisphere, and the instrument connected to them shows the magnitude of the force that each body exerts on the hemisphere with which it comes into contact.

The student, on reaching the top of the hill, has at his disposal several identical bodies, each of mass m, of negligible dimensions.

(A) The student gently pushes one of the above bodies from the top A of the hemisphere towards its right half. Determine the region of the hemisphere in which the instrument connected to the sensors will show a non-zero reading.

(B) What is the velocity with which the student must launch horizontally a body of mass m, from those at his disposal, from the top A of the hemisphere towards the side of the smooth surface, so that during its motion the sensors are not "activated" (that is, the reading of the instrument is zero) and it strikes the horizontal plane, at I, which lies R lower than the launch point, at the closest distance to the above-ground point Γ (of the front view) of the hemisphere (that is, ΓΙ minimum, corresponding to the optimum launch)? (See Figure 2.)

The radius R of the hemisphere and the acceleration of gravity g are given.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2025-2-3-fig2.png

[ΣΧΗΜΑ 2 = Figure 2.]

(C) At a height h > 3 m, on the same vertical as the highest point A of the hemisphere, ends the lowest point Η of a canopy (see front view, Figure 3). A tool of negligible dimensions and mass m slips out of the hands of a worker doing maintenance on the canopy, with no initial velocity, at the point Σ of the roof. The roof (canopy) that the worker is maintaining is part of a cylinder. The front face of the roof is a vertical semicircle of centre Ο and radius r. The points Ο, Σ, Α lie in the same plane (front view of Figure 3); the points Ο, Η, Α, Κ lie on the same vertical.

Explain the reading of the instrument of the sensitive sensors of the hemisphere due to the worker's accident.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2025-2-3-fig3.png

[Labels in the figure: ΠΡΟΣΟΨΗ ΣΚΕΠΑΣΤΡΟ ΚΥΚΛΙΚΟ ΗΜΙΣΦΑΙΡΙΟ = front view, circular canopy, hemisphere; ΤΡΑΧΙΑ ΕΠΙΦΑΝΕΙΑ μ=1 = rough surface μ = 1; ΣΧΗΜΑ 3 = Figure 3.]

The central angle ΣΟΗ = 60° and the coefficient of kinetic friction μ = 1, which is equal to the coefficient of limiting (static) friction, are given.

(D) Calculate the distance between the mark I on the horizontal plane (which lies R below the launch point) left by the body of mass m launched horizontally by the student when he has achieved the optimum launch, and the position of the tool that slipped from the worker when the speed of the tool is zero for the second time.

The calculation of the distance is to be made assuming that the kinetic friction has a constant magnitude equal to the minimum that it can take on the concave part ΣΗ of the roof.

Consider also that for the equation $\cos(\pi/3+\alpha) = (1-\alpha)/2$ one has $\alpha = -0.95$.

Given: g, R, h > 3 m, m, coefficient of kinetic friction μ = 1, which is equal to the coefficient of limiting friction, and r = 2 m.

problems.title: Problem 4
problems.problem:
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2025-2-4-fig1.png

The sphere of mass $m_1$, moving horizontally with speed of magnitude $u_1 = 10\,\mathrm{m/s}$, collides centrally with the stationary $(u_2 = 0)$ sphere of mass $m_2$ $(m_2 = 3m_1)$, which hangs from a massless string of fixed length $\ell = 0.5\,\mathrm{m}$, whose other end is fixed at point O, which is at a distance $H = 20\,\mathrm{m}$ from the horizontal ground. Immediately after the collision the sphere of mass $m_2$ acquires just enough kinetic energy to only just complete a vertical circle (loop).

(D1) Calculate the speed of the sphere of mass $m_2$ at its highest position during its vertical circle.

(D2) Calculate the velocities $u'_1$ and $u'_2$ of the two spheres respectively immediately after the collision.

(D3) Calculate the point at which, and the velocity with which, the sphere of mass $m_1$ meets the ground.

(D4) Prove that during the collision of the spheres there was no loss of energy.

(D5) Calculate the percentage of the initial kinetic energy of the sphere of mass $m_1$ that was received by the sphere $m_2$.

Consider resistances negligible. Given $g = 10\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$.

problems.title: Problem 5
problems.problem:
A group of students with their teacher want to investigate experimentally the Principle of Conservation of Mechanical Energy and the Principle of Independence of Motions.

They have a curved track which can accelerate a small sphere (photograph). At the end of the track the sphere acquires a horizontal velocity υ and performs a horizontal projectile motion from a height H = 0.25 m, as shown in the figure. The sphere is released from different heights y above the base of the track and, after acquiring a horizontal velocity υ at the end of the track, performs a horizontal projectile motion. When it reaches the floor we measure the horizontal distance x of the horizontal projectile motion.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2025-2-5-fig1.jpg

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2025-2-5-fig2.png

We release the sphere from different heights y and, after it has been accelerated by the track and performed a horizontal projectile motion, we measure the horizontal displacement x of the horizontal projectile motion.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c} \text{No.} & y\,(\mathrm{m}) & x\,(\mathrm{m}) \\ \hline 1 & 0.00 & 0.00 \\ 2 & 0.02 & 0.12 \\ 3 & 0.04 & 0.16 \\ 4 & 0.06 & 0.21 \\ 5 & 0.08 & 0.24 \\ 6 & 0.10 & 0.26 \end{array}$$

A. Find theoretically, using the Principle of conservation of mechanical energy and the principle of independence of motions, the function y = f(x). (Ignore friction, air resistance and the rotation of the sphere.)

What shape do you predict the graph y = f(x) will have?

B. Draw the graph of the experimental data of y as a function of x. Is the theoretical prediction of question A confirmed?

C. Transform the experimental data y and x so that the graph is a straight line. Draw the new graph.

D. What is the physical meaning of the slope of the 2nd graph?

E. Calculate the height H of the horizontal projectile motion from the 2nd graph and compare it with the theoretical value. Is there a difference, and if so, state two causes.

Roundings are to be made to two decimal places.

problems.title: Problem 2
problems.problem:

At the instant $t_o = 0$, when the balloon is at a height Η equal to $H = 120\,\mathrm{m}$, an object is launched vertically upwards from the ground with initial velocity $u_o = 50\,\mathrm{\frac{m}{s}}$, with the aim of this object being collected with a grapple (a tool with a hook) at the instants when it passes very close to the balloon.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2025-3-2-fig1.png

A. At what instant must the people in the balloon try to catch the object?

C. At what height will these attempts take place?

D. If all the attempts fail, at what height will the balloon be when the object returns to the ground?

Given $g = 10\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$.

problems.title: Problem 3
problems.problem:
On the surface of an inclined plane of inclination φ, the bodies $\Sigma_1$ of mass $m_1 = 1\,\mathrm{kg}$ and $\Sigma_2$ of mass $m_2 = 3\,\mathrm{kg}$ are held at rest at a distance $\ell = 3.6\,\mathrm{m}$ apart. https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2025-3-3-fig1.png

problems.title: Problem 5
problems.problem:
One of the most entertaining experiences in amusement parks is the drop in a drop tower, which is often referred to as a free-fall tower (Picture 1).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2025-3-5-fig1.jpg

Picture 1: A "free"-fall tower

The aim of this exercise is to check whether the fall in the tower is free. For this purpose a short part of the motion of the base (gondola) on the tower has been recorded on video, starting from the instant its motion begins. The video has been analysed with the help of the video-analysis software Tracker, and we have obtained the position (y) – time (t) data recorded in Table 1.

Table 1: Experimental data

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c} \text{No.} & t\ (\mathrm{s}) & y\ (\mathrm{m}) & t^2\ (\mathrm{s^2}) \\ \hline 1 & 0.0 & 0.0 & \\ 2 & 0.2 & 0.1 & \\ 3 & 0.4 & 0.5 & \\ 4 & 0.6 & 1.1 & \\ 5 & 0.8 & 2.0 & \\ 6 & 1.0 & 3.2 & \\ 7 & 1.2 & 4.6 & \end{array}$$

A. On the basis of the experimental values you observe in Table 1, justify that the motion of the base is not uniform but accelerated.

B. Fill in, in Table 1, the column with the squares of the instants of time. As you will use these data later, and to avoid rounding errors, keep two decimal places.

C. Draw on millimetre (graph) paper the graph $y = f(t^2)$. What form does the best-fit curve to the experimental data have? What does this mean for the kind of motion of the base in the drop tower?

D. Can you calculate the acceleration of the fall in the tower? In what way? Give your result and the necessary calculations. In the end, is the fall in the drop tower "free"?

The acceleration of gravity is given as $g = 9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$.

problems.problem:
A conducting rectangular frame of length $a$ and width $b$ carries a current $I$ and is placed with its plane parallel to the field lines of a uniform magnetic field of magnitude $\vec{B}$.

The disc is placed at the middle of a rod of length equal to $d$ and negligible mass which passes through its centre. The ends Κ and Λ of the rod rest on two supports and the plane of the disc is vertical. The system is placed in a vertical uniform magnetic field of magnitude $\vec{B}$ and the loop carries a current $I$. In correspondence with the answer to question (b), find:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2026-5-fig2.png

(c$_2$) What is the maximum value of the current such that contact is not lost. $g$ is given.
